<result># Research Findings: ra_ap_syntax vs syn, Salsa, and Rust Tokenization

## A. Bounding `ra_ap_syntax` parse-only throughput

No published number exists — confirmed harder. Checked directly: rust-analyzer's `crates/syntax` has no `benches/` directory at all ([GitHub API listing](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/tree/master/crates/syntax) — only `Cargo.toml`, `fuzz/`, `rust.ungram`, `src/`, `test_data/`). The historic ["Parsing seems slow" issue #1643](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/issues/1643) diagnosed redundant `Parser::nth` lookahead and Arc-drop overhead but published no throughput figure. The 2024 [issue #17491 "A Plan for Making Rust Analyzer Faster"](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/issues/17491) contains the "twice as slow as syntree" claim verbatim (contributor davidbarsky, benchmarking *tree construction only*, explicitly caveated as unfair since rowan's structural sharing serves incremental editing that syntree doesn't do) plus the "lack of mechanical sympathy" critique (heap-allocated Arcs, overused hashing, underused indexing, no identifier interning). `rowan`'s own repo/docs publish no benchmarks.

Two adjacent anchors help bound it. [tree-sitter-rust](https://github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter/discussions/3429) — also a lossless, error-recovering CST parser — is reported ~3x slower than rustc's hand-written parser. [`syn`](https://fasterthanli.me/articles/the-virtue-of-unsynn), an AST-only parser assuming valid input, is anecdotally reported parsing ~11,000 lines in ~100ms in a warm-build context — not a rigorous MB/s figure, but a real data point (order of ~100K+ lines/sec). No apples-to-apples benchmark of `ra_ap_syntax`/`rowan` against `syn` or tree-sitter-rust exists anywhere I could find.

**Best-bounded estimate:** lossless CST construction (trivia preservation, green/red tree, structural sharing) is inherently more work per token than `syn`'s AST-only parse of already-valid tokens. Combined with the 2x rowan-vs-syntree gap and tree-sitter's ~3x-vs-rustc gap, expect `ra_ap_syntax` to land in the same broad order of magnitude as tree-sitter-rust — plausibly 3–10x slower than `syn` per byte — likely low tens of MB/s on modern hardware rather than the ~100+ MB/s a bare AST parser could hit. For per-invocation CLI use over typical repo sizes (thousands of files, not gigabytes), this is probably still acceptable latency, but it is not free.

## B. `syn` as the structural-tier alternative

`syn` gives up exactly what the spec's questions predicted: no lossless trivia (comments/whitespace aren't first-class tree nodes the way ra_ap_syntax's CST preserves them for verbatim block-text reproduction), and no incremental reparse (moot here since monokl's Rust tier is cold per-invocation anyway). The sharper, *practical* concern is error recovery. `syn::File::parse` fails fast: [`syn::parse::Error`](https://docs.rs/syn/latest/syn/parse/struct.Error.html) documents returning `Err` at the first bad token, with the recommended pattern being to emit `compile_error!` and stop — there is no "give me what parsed and mark the rest broken" mode. `ra_ap_syntax` is IDE-designed specifically to always produce a tree, tagging error nodes rather than aborting. For monokl, which searches real working trees — WIP branches, merge-conflict markers, mid-edit files — a single syntax error anywhere in a `.rs` file would make `syn` yield zero symbols for that entire file, while `ra_ap_syntax` keeps extracting symbols around the error. That is a real regression, not a theoretical one.

## C. Salsa as monokl's own cache, independent of `ra_ap_hir`

Salsa is a generic, IR-agnostic memoized-query engine, not coupled to rust-analyzer's data model. Two concrete precedents of standalone use: Astral's **ty** (formerly red-knot) Python type checker built its own Salsa-based incremental system from scratch, independent of rust-analyzer's queries ([talkpython.fm](https://talkpython.fm/episodes/show/506/ty-astrals-new-type-checker-formerly-red-knot), [DeepWiki](https://deepwiki.com/astral-sh/ruff/6-red-knot-type-checker)); and **Biome**, a JS/TS linter/formatter toolchain in a domain adjacent to monokl's, uses Salsa in its workspace/analyzer layer (evidenced by a recent [salsa-setter deadlock fix](https://github.com/biomejs/biome/commit/6450276764ee4794a0fcb46c139f95b68d892427)). Monokl could define its own queries (symbols-for-file, postings-for-term) memoized on content hash, without touching `cargo metadata`/crate-graph machinery — a materially lighter proposition than embedding `ra_ap_hir`. Caveat: Salsa's API has undergone significant breaking rewrites; pin a version deliberately.

## D. Tokenizer, grounded in `tokens.rs` (monokl-spec.md:866-937)

Traced each construct against the actual code. `vec!`/`println!` → `!` is a pure separator, base identifier survives as "vec"/"println" (fine). Turbofish `::<Vec<u8>>` → `::`/`<`/`>` are separators, inner identifiers tokenize normally, single-letter generics (`T`) correctly dropped by the len≥2 filter. `#[derive(Debug, Clone)]` → tokens "derive", "debug", "clone" — meaningfully indexed, contrary to worry. Confirmed gap: `'a` is dropped as noise (apostrophe separates, "a" is len-1). Longer lifetimes (`'ctx`, `'static`) survive but collide indistinguishably with plain identifiers — minor precision loss. A real, cheap-to-fix gap: `STOP_WORDS` includes `mod`/`impl`/`pub`/`type` etc. but omits `crate`, `self`, `super`, `dyn`, `async`, `await`, `unsafe` — these will appear as high-frequency near-universal tokens across any Rust corpus (BM25's IDF partially compensates, but it's free precision left on the table). Edge case: raw identifiers (`r#type`) vanish entirely since the escaped keyword is itself a stopword.

## Recommendation

Keep `ra_ap_syntax` for the structural tier. Its error recovery on malformed/in-progress code is a load-bearing feature for a search tool scanning real working trees, not a nice-to-have — `syn`'s fail-fast model would silently blank out symbol extraction for any file with a syntax error, which is worse than the unquantified throughput cost of the CST. Investigate Salsa separately and independently of the `ra_ap_hir` question — it has real standalone precedent (ty, Biome) and would give monokl warm-daemon-style incremental recomputation for its own queries without a crate-graph load. For the tokenizer, add `crate`, `self`, `super`, `dyn`, `async`, `await`, `unsafe` to `STOP_WORDS` as a low-cost precision improvement; no other change is warranted.</result>

validates design

codegraph's Python extractor is genuinely thin — 53 lines against Rust's 152 — with only four hand-written hooks (type-hint signatures, async detection, a purely textual @staticmethod check rather than real decorator resolution, and import mapping). No dedicated __all__ handling, no real decorator resolution, no dunder-method special-casing — all of it falls to the generic tree-walking engine. The implicit rationale: Python's grammar is structurally regular enough that hand-tuning barely pays for itself. That's a reasonable precedent for monokl's own future Python analyzer to lean generic-first rather than front-load logic the way the TS analyzer does.

Rust's extractor is comparably sophisticated to TypeScript's — real handling for chained-builder return-type normalization, impl/impl Trait for X receiver-type resolution including generics, recursive use-path unwrapping. But it has zero lifetime handling and zero macro modeling — macro_rules!/macro_invocation appear nowhere in its type lists. Even a mature, production, issue-hardened tool just punts on Rust macros entirely.

Independent convergent validation: codegraph's cargo-workspace.ts resolves cross-crate use crate_name::... paths via a workspace package-root map — the same concept monokl's spec already has (resolve_rust_path + package_roots), arrived at separately. Even a well-resourced team reached for the full type checker rather than approximate it. That's good validation that Structural precision (not Exact) is the pragmatic, well-precedented v1.1 target, not corner-cutting.

Pyright resolves __all__ and re-exports at the binder phase, before type inference — genuinely cheap, syntax-level work, directly supporting Structural-tier implementation of two of the spec's six open Python questions without a type checker. keep ra_ap_syntax

No published ra_ap_syntax parse-only throughput exists anywhere, confirmed harder this round — rust-analyzer's own crates/syntax doesn't even have a benches/ directory. Reasoning from adjacent data points (rowan reported ~2× slower than syntree for tree construction alone; tree-sitter-rust, a comparably lossless parser, runs ~3× slower than rustc's hand-written parser), a defensible bound is low tens of MB/s — plausibly 3–10× slower than syn.

Why that cost is probably worth paying: syn::File::parse fails fast — it returns Err at the first bad token with no partial-parse mode, the documented pattern being to emit compile_error! and stop. ra_ap_syntax is IDE-designed to always produce a tree, tagging error nodes instead of aborting. Monokl searches real working trees — WIP branches, merge-conflict markers, mid-edit files. A single syntax error anywhere in a .rs file would make syn yield zero symbols for that entire file. That's a real regression, not a theoretical one — the unquantified throughput cost of keeping ra_ap_syntax is the better trade.

A genuinely new option surfaced: Salsa, rust-analyzer's incremental-computation engine, is architecturally independent of ra_ap_hir — it has real standalone precedent (Astral's ty Python type checker and Biome's analyzer layer both use it decoupled from rust-analyzer's own queries). Monokl could define its own memoized queries — symbols-for-file, postings-for-term — without ever loading a crate graph via cargo metadata. A materially lighter middle ground than thread 07's daemon-or-nothing framing, worth its own investigation track independent of the ra_ap_hir decision.

Tokenizer check, traced against the actual code: macro invocations, turbofish, and derive-attribute contents all tokenize sensibly, contrary to worry. Two real gaps: short lifetimes ('a) are dropped as noise by the length filter, and STOP_WORDS omits crate, self, super, dyn, async, await, unsafe — near-universal tokens across any Rust corpus, free precision left on the table.

  • docs.rs/syn — parse::Error

What other languages should we consider?

Two different questions are bundled in "what other languages" — and they have different answers:

**Is the current roadmap (TS/JS → Rust/Python → C#) right?** Probably yes, and not by guesswork — the spec's own references (an ADR for `proto-dotnet`/`orbit`, `Broadway.Marketplace` fixtures) point to C# reflecting a real internal codebase at the company, not a speculative market-coverage pick. That's the right kind of signal to expand on.

**Should monokl add languages beyond those four?** Here's the more interesting strategic finding from everything we just learned about codegraph: monokl commits to a fully-native parser per language (OXC, ra-ap-syntax) — precise, but each new language is a real engineering project, not a config file. codegraph gets to 30+ languages cheaply because it's one generic tree-sitter-walking engine with thin per-language config objects bolted on. Monokl's own `AnalyzerCapabilities`/`CapabilityPrecision` model was *designed* for exactly this kind of tradeoff — it already expects analyzers to vary in precision. The move that actually fits the architecture isn't "pick language #5," it's **deciding whether to add a generic tree-sitter fallback tier** (`Heuristic` or `Structural` precision, search/symbols only, no bespoke semantic layer) for the long tail, while reserving native-parser investment for languages that earn it.

That reframes the real question back to you: is language priority here driven by **StubHub's actual internal codebases** (in which case — what else runs there besides TS/JS, Rust, and C#? Go or Java for backend services? Something else?), or by **monokl becoming a broader tool** where general market share (Go, Java are the obvious next two) matters more? I can't tell which from the spec alone, and it changes what's worth researching next.

input.description: Research Go language support for monokl
input.prompt:
Context: "monokl" is a Rust code-search/analysis tool for AI coding agents, currently spec'd for TypeScript/JavaScript (via native OXC parser crates), Rust (via native ra_ap_syntax), and Python (via tree-sitter-python, per prior research this session — Ruff's own Rust-native parser crates were found to be explicitly unstable/not viable). We're now evaluating Go as a candidate 4th language, targeting general market reach rather than one company's internal stack. The established pattern for evaluating each language this session has been: (1) does a mature NATIVE Rust parser crate exist as a lighter/faster alternative to tree-sitter, or is tree-sitter-go the only practical option; (2) what does real semantic analysis (name resolution, package-aware symbol binding) cost, and is it daemon-only or embeddable in a cold CLI invocation; (3) how does a real production multi-language tool (colbymchenry/codegraph, cloned locally) actually handle this language today; (4) what are the language-specific tokenization concerns for BM25 search ranking.

Please research and report on:

**A. Native Rust Go-parser landscape.** Search crates.io and GitHub for Rust crates that parse Go source into an AST/CST (not FFI-wrapping the real Go toolchain, not shelling out to `go` — a genuine Rust-native parser, analogous to how `syn` parses Rust or how OXC parses TS/JS). Candidates to check specifically: any crate literally named something like `gosyn`, `go-parser`, `goast`, etc. Assess maturity (last publish date, download count, whether it's a hobby project or has real adoption), and whether it handles modern Go correctly (generics, added in Go 1.18 — a common gap in older/abandoned Go parsers). If nothing viable exists, say so plainly rather than stretching a marginal crate into a recommendation.

**B. Go semantic-analysis cost model.** `gopls` (the official Go language server) and the `golang.org/x/tools/go/packages` / `go/analysis` stack do real package-aware type-checking and resolution, but are themselves Go programs (not embeddable in a Rust binary without shelling out or FFI). Research: what's the actual cost of `go/packages.Load()` for a mid-size Go module (any published benchmarks, gopls startup-time discussions on their issue tracker, blog posts)? Is there a lighter, syntax-only Go analysis path analogous to what monokl does for Rust (parse + structural extraction, no semantic resolution) that doesn't require shelling out to `go` at all? Go's package/import resolution is comparatively simpler than Rust's (no macros, no generic monomorphization complexity at the syntax level, and Go modules have a well-defined `go.mod` + `GOPATH`/module-cache layout) — does that make Go import resolution meaningfully easier to do heuristically/structurally (mirroring monokl's `resolve_rust_path` pattern) than Rust's, or are there real gotchas (build tags/`//go:build` constraints changing which files are even part of a build, vendoring, workspace `go.work` files)?

**C. How codegraph actually handles Go, read from source.** The repo is cloned at `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gabe-Projects-monokl/a82f4f80-7822-4785-a872-33c66baeee45/scratchpad/codegraph`. Check `src/extraction/languages/go.ts` (or similarly named) if it exists — read it in full, not grepped — and compare its sophistication/hand-tuning to what's already known about codegraph's TypeScript extractor (heavily hand-tuned, ~many custom hooks) versus its Python extractor (thin, ~53 lines, leans on the generic engine). Also check `src/resolution/frameworks/` for any Go-specific framework resolver (e.g. for Gin, Echo, or other common Go web frameworks) and `src/resolution/` for Go-specific import/module resolution logic (does it handle `go.mod`/`go.work` workspace resolution the way it handles Rust's Cargo workspaces via `cargo-workspace.ts`?).

**D. Go-specific tokenization for BM25.** monokl's tokenizer splits on non-alphanumeric chars, breaks camelCase, treats `_`/`-` as hard delimiters, filters tokens shorter than 2 chars, and has a stop-word list. Go idioms to consider: short variable names are idiomatic in Go (`err`, `ctx`, `wg`, `i`) — would the length≥2 filter wrongly suppress meaningful 2-char idiomatic names, or is that fine since single-char names are already filtered and 2-char ones like `wg`/`ok` survive? Struct tags (`` `json:"name,omitempty"` ``) — would backtick-delimited tag strings tokenize sensibly or produce noise? Go's own stop-word candidates (`func`, `package`, `import`, `interface`, `struct`, `chan`, `go`, `defer`, `select` — is monokl's current generic STOP_WORDS list, tuned for TS/Rust, missing obvious Go keywords the same way it was found to be missing Rust keywords like `crate`/`dyn`/`async`?).

Report back under 700 words, organized markdown, citations for external claims, ending with a concrete recommendation: does Go get a native structural-tier analyzer (mirroring Rust/TS's approach) or does it belong in a generic tree-sitter fallback tier, and what CapabilityPrecision level (Unsupported/Heuristic/Structural/Exact) is realistic for a v1 Go integration.

# Part 5: Pre-implementation research amendments

> Added before any of Parts 1-4 have been built. A competitive deep-dive against
> colbymchenry/codegraph (a mature, production multi-language code-intelligence tool) plus
> targeted follow-on research were used to stress-test this spec's assumptions before they
> calcify into code. Two categories below: fixes already applied directly to the sections
> above, and decisions/open tracks that change what future PRs should do.

## 1. Fixes applied in this document

- **§Python fidelity, problem 5** (type annotation resolution): `CapabilityPrecision::Approximate`
  was not a real variant of the enum defined in §11 (`Unsupported < Heuristic < Structural <
  Exact`). Corrected to `CapabilityPrecision::Heuristic`.
- **§Section 6, `STOP_WORDS`**: added `crate`, `self`, `super`, `dyn`, `async`, `await`, `unsafe`
  — near-universal Rust tokens the original TS/Rust-tuned list omitted, found by tracing the
  tokenizer's actual splitting rules against real Rust source rather than assuming coverage.

## 2. Adopted, not yet implemented

- **Add `oxc_semantic` to the `lang-ts` feature's dependency set**, versioned in lockstep with
  `oxc_parser`/`oxc_ast`/`oxc_span`/`oxc_allocator` (same version string — no separate
  compatibility matrix). `SemanticBuilder::build(&program)` runs against the same per-file
  `Allocator` arena the parser already uses and produces a `Semantic` result (scope tree +
  symbol table: `SymbolId`/`ScopeId`/`Reference`, real shadowing/hoisting/TDZ-aware binding).
  This replaces regex/text-scanned local-usage resolution in `refs`/`definition` with genuine
  scope-aware resolution for within-file references — closing the exact class of technical debt
  codegraph's own maintainers flag as their worst (a 20+-resolver heuristic confidence cascade).
  `oxc_semantic` is file-scoped: it does not replace `oxc_resolver` for cross-file specifier
  resolution, it upgrades what feeds into that combination. Output must be converted to owned
  data before the arena drops, same discipline as the AST conversion already documented in §17.
- **Build an eval harness before further ranking/tuning decisions are made on faith.** BM25's
  `K1=1.5`/`B=0.5` and the token-budget defaults are carried over from Probe's prior tuning
  (§29) and are unvalidated for monokl specifically. Minimum viable harness: two layers, not
  one — (a) a deterministic retrieval eval (RepoBench-R- or CodeSearchNet-style recall@k/MRR)
  run on every commit, and (b) a properly-powered agent A/B (model/effort pinned and logged,
  ≥5 runs per condition reporting median + IQR, ≥10 repos with a task list frozen before either
  arm runs). Report token and dollar-cost deltas *separately*, broken out by cache-read vs.
  fresh-input token mix — codegraph's own published cost-savings claim reversed under
  independent replication specifically because token/call reductions and dollar cost decoupled
  when its context payload shifted from many cheap cached reads to fewer expensive fresh reads.
  Cheapest first step: fill in the four already-stubbed `benches/pipeline.rs` criterion groups
  (`pipeline_cold`, `pipeline_warm_cache`, `dependents_warm`, `lite_symbols`, §29) — every
  cold/warm latency target asserted elsewhere in this spec is currently unmeasured, including
  in monokl's own benchmark suite.
- **Add worked query examples and a tolerant natural-language fallback** to the `search`
  command's tool-facing description. The `+/-/"phrase"/regex:` grammar itself is confirmed
  well-matched to how coding agents actually call lexical search tools (every purpose-built tool
  surveyed — Claude Code's Grep, Cline, Continue.dev, GitHub's MCP `search_code` — uses
  regex/qualifier syntax; natural language appears only as a separate, explicitly-labeled
  semantic tool elsewhere, never mixed into a grep-style tool's input). The gap is discoverability,
  not grammar: detect question-like input (`where`/`how`/`?`, five-plus words, no `+`/`-`/`regex:`
  modifiers) and degrade gracefully to bare-optional-term matching instead of erroring, since
  agents will occasionally route full questions to any tool that sounds like "search."

## 3. Validated — no change made

- **`ra_ap_syntax` stays over `syn`** for the Rust structural tier. `syn::File::parse` fails fast
  at the first bad token with no partial-parse mode (the documented pattern is to emit
  `compile_error!` and stop); `ra_ap_syntax` is IDE-designed to always produce a tree, tagging
  error nodes instead. Monokl searches real working trees — WIP branches, merge-conflict
  markers, mid-edit files — where a single syntax error under `syn` would blank out symbol
  extraction for that entire file. No published throughput number for `ra_ap_syntax` parse-only
  performance exists anywhere (confirmed absent even in rust-analyzer's own benchmark suite);
  the error-recovery gap is the deciding factor regardless of the unquantified speed cost.
- **`tree-sitter-python` stays over Ruff's Rust-native parser crates** for `lang-py`.
  `ruff_python_ast`/`ruff_python_parser` are explicitly disclaimed by Ruff itself as unstable
  internal implementation details (still `0.0.x`, "frequent breaking changes" in their own
  words) — not a publishable dependency contract. tree-sitter-python's actual open issues
  cluster around bleeding-edge type-hint syntax (PEP 604/695), not the decorators/classes/
  `__all__` handling the Python fidelity questions above actually need.
- **`WorkspaceIndex::build`'s parallel-analyze-then-sort-by-path pattern needs no upgrade** to a
  strict sequential-commit scheme. That extra machinery exists in comparable tools only to
  compensate for heuristic name-matching resolvers that disambiguate same-named candidates by
  database insertion order — monokl doesn't have that failure mode, because `oxc_resolver` and
  `resolve_rust_path` resolve each import to a specific file deterministically (no name-based
  candidate list to tie-break), and everywhere else multiple candidates can occur
  (`SymbolIndex::lookup`, `definition`'s re-export ranking) this spec already sorts on explicit
  keys — path, line, re-export flag — not insertion order.

## 4. Open investigation tracks — not decided

- **Salsa** (rust-analyzer's incremental-computation engine) as monokl's own memoized
  query cache, decoupled from any `ra_ap_hir` decision. Real standalone precedent exists
  (Astral's `ty` Python type checker, Biome's analyzer layer both use Salsa independent of
  rust-analyzer's own queries) — monokl could define its own queries (symbols-for-file,
  postings-for-term) memoized on content hash without ever loading a crate graph, a materially
  lighter proposition than embedding `ra_ap_hir` wholesale. Worth a scoped spike, tracked
  separately from the item below.
- **`ra_ap_hir` integration and any persistent daemon/session mode are a coupled pair.**
  `ra_ap_hir`'s `Semantics` gives real Rust name resolution and type inference, but needs a
  populated `HirDatabase` via `cargo metadata` + crate-graph construction — a cost pegged by
  rust-analyzer's own maintainers at roughly 5 seconds per 100 crates just waiting on rustc.
  That cost model fits a warm, long-lived process, not a cold per-invocation CLI. Symmetrically,
  a persistent index/daemon mode (mirroring codegraph's watcher architecture) only earns its
  own cost past roughly 50k files — below that, the current stateless design's per-invocation
  fold cost (re-aggregating already-cached per-file analyses into `ImportGraph`/`SymbolIndex`,
  not re-parsing) is estimated at 100-500ms at 10k files and 300ms-1.5s at 50k, a small fraction
  of the 15s cold-build budget. Revisit both together, after the eval harness (§2) and the
  stubbed benchmarks (§2) produce real numbers — not before.
- **Over-fetch-then-rerank staging** in the search pipeline is the one ranking pattern with real
  cross-tool evidence (Continue.dev, codegraph, general two-stage IR) beyond what §Section 8
  already does; a small import/reference-proximity nudge as a minor multiplier is defensible.
  Scope not yet decided — do not build a full Aider-style PageRank-over-symbols system as a
  primary rank driver on this basis; Aider's own repo-map algorithm has no published evidence it
  beats simpler baselines despite being well engineered.

## 5. Rejected

- **Embedding-based semantic rerank by default.** No code-specific evidence shows it beats
  lexical+structural signals for single-codebase retrieval (identifiers matter more than
  paraphrase within one codebase), and every tool surveyed that uses it depends on server-side
  vector-DB infrastructure — none of the local-first CLI tools examined run it by default. If
  ever added, gate behind an explicit opt-in flag; it is not this spec's default posture.

## 6. Language roadmap

The v1.2 target of C# is dropped. Priority beyond `lang-ts`/`lang-rs`/`lang-py` is now driven by
general market reach rather than one company's internal stack, with Go and Java as the leading
candidates (research in flight as of this writing — findings pending). A related architectural
question raised by studying codegraph (which reaches 30+ languages via one generic
tree-sitter-walking engine with thin per-language config, versus monokl's fully-native
per-language analyzer approach): whether to add a generic tree-sitter fallback tier —
`Heuristic`/`Structural` precision only, search/symbols capability without a bespoke semantic
layer — for the long tail, reserving native-parser investment (the OXC/ra-ap-syntax/
tree-sitter-python pattern) for languages that earn it. Not yet decided; tracked alongside the
Go/Java findings.

Java's back, and it settled cleanly:

- **No viable native Rust Java parser exists** — checked `oak-java` and `java-lang` specifically (both single-maintainer, pre-1.0, near-zero organic adoption). - **Explicit FQN imports cut both ways**: non-wildcard imports give an unambiguous textual mapping (easier than Go/TS), but idiomatic Java leans much more heavily on JAR-only external symbols (JDK, Spring, Guava, Lombok) with no local source than comparable Rust/Python code does — a structurally harder version of a gap monokl already has elsewhere.

<result># Go as monokl's 4th Language — Research Findings

## A. Native Rust Go-parser landscape

**gosyn** ([chikaku/gosyn](https://github.com/chikaku/gosyn)) is real and viable, contrary to expectations for a niche parser: 152,004 downloads, 17 published versions since Feb 2022, last crates.io publish 2026-07-14 (days old), commits weekly, MIT-licensed, 33 stars/7 forks, 3 real downstream dependents. Source confirms Go 1.18+ generics support — `parse_type_parameters()`, `type_parameters()`, and tests for generic instantiation/generic pointer types all exist. This is the strongest native-parser candidate found across all four languages evaluated this session.

By contrast: **go-parser/go-types** (Goscript project) explicitly excludes generics ("pre-1.18... excluding generics") and the whole project is now unmaintained, superseded by Volang. **golang-parser** (bk-rs/golang-rs) is a struct-tag-to-Rust-struct converter, not a general parser (13 stars). **gofmt** (zjykzk) is a brand-new (Oct 2025, 594 downloads) formatter, unproven. **gomod-rs/gomod-parser** only parse `go.mod`, not source. No "goast" Rust crate exists.

## B. Semantic-analysis cost model

`go/packages.Load` scales with package count, not embeddable in a cold CLI call: on a 20k-package monorepo (77,688 files), `InitialWorkspaceLoadDuration` was **3m26s** cold, with `go list` alone taking 1m6s ([golang/go#69523](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/69523)). Even a *warm* gopls daemon serving a new client on a 2,047-package repo took 10+ seconds before becoming usable ([golang/go#48829](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/48829)). This confirms daemon-only architecture, same conclusion as Rust's `ra_ap_hir`.

A lighter, syntax-only path is exactly monokl's existing Rust pattern (parse + structural extraction, no resolution) — directly portable via gosyn, since Go's own `go/parser`/`go/ast` are Go-only and using them at all means cgo/FFI, which monokl wants to avoid.

Import resolution *is* easier than Rust's for the common case — codegraph's own `resolveGoCrossPackageReference` proves it out today: read `go.mod`'s module directive, strip the prefix from an import path to get a project-relative directory, look up the exported symbol. No macros, no monomorphization. Real gotchas: (1) **go.work** — codegraph's `go-module.ts` explicitly reads only the root `go.mod` and documents nested/workspace modules as unhandled; (2) **build tags** — gopls auto-resolves the filename-suffix convention (`_linux.go`, `_amd64.go`) but explicitly cannot auto-detect arbitrary `//go:build mytag` constraints ([gopls workspace docs](https://github.com/golang/tools/blob/master/gopls/doc/workspace.md)), so a structural tool will see phantom duplicate symbol definitions across tag-gated files; (3) vendoring has no Go-specific handling in codegraph, only generic gitignore-negation.

## C. codegraph's Go handling (read in full)

Go gets real hand-tuned investment, closer to TS than to the thin Python tier. `extraction/languages/go.ts` (105 lines): custom return-type unwrapping (pointer/multi-return/generic-arg stripping), receiver-type regex handling generic receivers `(s *Stack[T])`, uppercase-first-letter export detection — comparable to `rust.ts` (151 lines), well beyond `python.ts` (53 lines, no return-type/receiver logic at all).

Go has **two** framework resolvers: `frameworks/go.ts` (Gin/Echo/Fiber/Chi/net-http route detection including Go 1.22 `"METHOD /path"` patterns) and `frameworks/goframe.ts` (GoFrame's reflective `g.Meta` struct-tag routing, joined via a separate synthesizer). `resolution/go-module.ts` is a dedicated `go.mod` parser mirroring `cargo-workspace.ts`'s role, but simpler — single-file only, no glob member expansion like Cargo's `members=["crates/*"]`. `import-resolver.ts` contains real Go-specific logic (`isExternalImport` go-branch, `resolveGoCrossPackageReference`) directly analogous to `resolve_rust_path`. No `go.work` support exists anywhere (confirmed by grep).

## D. BM25 tokenization for Go

Length≥2 filter is fine — single-char idioms (i,j,k) are filtered equally in every language; 2-char idioms (`wg`, `ok`, `db`, `tx`) and 3-char (`err`, `ctx`) survive untouched. Struct tags tokenize cleanly since backticks/colons/quotes are delimiters: `` `json:"name,omitempty"` `` → json/name/omitempty — sensible, if low-IDF. monokl's STOP_WORDS is TS/Rust-tuned and misses Go keywords the same way it missed Rust's crate/dyn/async: absent are `func`, `package`, `chan`, `defer`, `select`, `range`, `go`, `iota`. `interface`/`struct` already present coincidentally help Go. `go` itself (2 chars, survives the filter) is Go's near-zero-IDF goroutine keyword and should be added.

## Recommendation

Give Go a **native structural tier**: gosyn as primary parser (tree-sitter-go as fallback, since codegraph already ships `tree-sitter-go.wasm`), heuristic `go.mod`-based import resolution mirroring `resolve_rust_path`, extended STOP_WORDS (`func`/`package`/`chan`/`defer`/`select`/`range`/`go`/`iota`), with `go.work` and `//go:build` resolution explicitly scoped out of v1 as documented gaps.

**CapabilityPrecision: Structural** — no type-checking, no build-tag-aware disambiguation, no workspace support, but well above Heuristic given gosyn's real AST and codegraph's proven `go.mod`-based cross-package resolution.</result>

## 6. Language roadmap

The v1.2 target of C# is dropped. Priority beyond `lang-ts`/`lang-rs`/`lang-py` is now driven by
general market reach rather than one company's internal stack. Go and Java were evaluated as
the leading candidates; both get a native `Structural`-tier analyzer, but via different parsers,
for reasons specific to each language's actual crate ecosystem (checked directly against
crates.io, not assumed):

**`lang-go`** — **`gosyn`** ([chikaku/gosyn](https://github.com/chikaku/gosyn)) is a real, viable
native Rust parser: 152k+ downloads, weekly commits, MIT-licensed, confirmed Go 1.18+ generics
support (`parse_type_parameters`, generic instantiation/pointer types both present in source and
tests). This is the strongest native-parser candidate found across every language evaluated this
session — unlike Python and Java, Go did not need to fall back to tree-sitter. `go/packages.Load`
(real semantic analysis) is daemon-only by the same argument as `ra_ap_hir`: a 20k-package
monorepo took 3m26s cold to load ([golang/go#69523](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/69523)),
and even a warm gopls daemon took 10+ seconds to serve a new client on a 2,047-package repo
([golang/go#48829](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/48829)). Import resolution is genuinely
easier than Rust's for the common case — no macros, no monomorphization, and a `go.mod` module
directive plus import-path-prefix-stripping gives a project-relative directory directly (mirror
`resolve_rust_path`'s shape, but simpler). Two gaps explicitly out of scope for v1: `go.work`
multi-module workspaces (unhandled — root `go.mod` only), and `//go:build`-tag-gated files
(gopls itself cannot auto-detect arbitrary build tags beyond the `_linux.go`-style filename
convention; a structural tool will see phantom duplicate symbols across tag-gated variants of
the same declaration). `CapabilityPrecision::Structural`. Tokenizer: extend `STOP_WORDS` with
`func`, `package`, `chan`, `defer`, `select`, `range`, `go`, `iota` when `lang-go` lands
(`new`/`super`/`interface`/`struct` are already covered by existing entries).

**`lang-java`** — no viable native Rust parser exists (`oak-java` and `java-lang` are both
single-maintainer, pre-1.0, near-zero organic adoption; no `java-parser`/`javasyn` crate exists
at all). `tree-sitter-java` is the correct choice, same conclusion as Python, and independently
confirmed by codegraph's own "native, no-WASM" performance kernel — even it compiles
`tree-sitter-java` natively via FFI rather than replacing the grammar. Real semantic analysis
(JDT/`javac` classpath resolution via `jdtls`) is daemon-only, with documented real-world pain at
scale (20s cold completion on multi-million-line projects vs. 1-2s warm,
[eclipse-jdtls/eclipse.jdt.ls#3202](https://github.com/eclipse-jdtls/eclipse.jdt.ls/issues/3202);
OOM crashes importing 3000+-file projects,
[#1469](https://github.com/eclipse-jdtls/eclipse.jdt.ls/issues/1469)) — unlike Rust/Go, there is
no established lightweight semi-semantic tier for Java at all; the field is bimodal. Non-wildcard
imports (`import com.foo.Bar;`) give an unambiguous textual simple-name→FQN mapping, easier than
Go's or Rust's equivalent case — but the majority of real-world Java imports (JDK, Spring, Guava,
Lombok) resolve to JAR-only symbols with no local source, a structural wall no non-JVM tool can
cross, and one that bites harder in Java than in Rust/TS/Go because idiomatic Java leans more
heavily on external-library symbols per file. Worth the same order of hand-tuning investment
codegraph put into its own Java extractor (334 lines — its most hand-tuned language after TS):
specifically Lombok-generated-member synthesis (`@Getter`/`@Setter`/`@Data`/`@Builder` → synthetic
getter/setter/`equals`/`hashCode` nodes), without which Lombok codegen silently breaks call-chain
resolution. No Maven/Gradle multi-module resolver exists even in mature production tools (a
documented gap, not an oversight) — cap that specific case at `Heuristic`.
`CapabilityPrecision::Structural` for same-module declarations and non-wildcard local import
resolution; `Heuristic` for wildcard imports, cross-JAR external symbols, and multi-module
source-root inference; `Exact` explicitly out of scope (daemon-only). Tokenizer: extend
`STOP_WORDS` with `public`, `private`, `protected`, `static`, `final`, `void`, `implements`,
`package`, `throws`, `abstract`, `instanceof`, `null` when `lang-java` lands (`new`/`super` are
already covered).

A related architectural question raised by studying codegraph (which reaches 30+ languages via
one generic tree-sitter-walking engine with thin per-language config, versus monokl's fully-native
per-language analyzer approach): whether to add a generic tree-sitter fallback tier —
`Heuristic`/`Structural` precision only, search/symbols capability without a bespoke semantic
layer — for languages beyond this list. Not yet decided; Go and Java themselves do not need it,

Monokl · Research Dossier

Result quality & performance — the codegraph comparison, followed to ground

Fourteen research threads, run to verify or kill assumptions in the monokl spec before any of it gets built. Adversarially checked where it mattered; honestly hedged where the evidence ran out.

Scope: codegraph deep-read, follow-on threads, TS/Rust/Python/Go/Java coverage Method: source-code reads, adversarial multi-source verification, back-of-envelope arithmetic Status: language roadmap + tokenizer fixes applied to the spec; rest pending
At a glance

Every thread below, one line each. Full reasoning and sources follow in order.

01 · codegraph, verified
mixed evidence
Architecturally sound and battle-tested, but its own headline benchmark numbers didn't survive independent replication.
02 · oxc_semantic / ra_ap_hir
adopt (TS/JS half)
oxc_semantic is a clear, low-cost upgrade. ra_ap_hir is real but needs a daemon — couples to thread 07.
03 · ranking beyond BM25
adopt narrowly
Over-fetch-then-rerank is well evidenced. Aider-style PageRank and embeddings are not — keep both out or minor.
04 · how agents query
grammar confirmed
Term-based grammar matches the field. Add worked examples and a natural-language fallback.
05 · eval harness
build it
codegraph's own cost numbers didn't replicate — a two-layer harness with dollar cost as a named metric avoids their exact mistake.
06 · scale & memory targets
mostly generous
TS/JS targets have huge headroom on real numbers. The Rust path has zero throughput validation.
07 · persistent session vs cold start
keep stateless
Fold cost is small next to LLM think-time at ≤50k files. A daemon only earns its keep past that.
08 · parallel-parse commit ordering
no change needed
Monokl already sidesteps the problem codegraph built extra machinery to solve.
09 · was Rust & Python actually covered?
gap, now closed
TS/JS dominated the first pass. Rust had two real flagged gaps; Python had none until this round.
10 · codegraph's Python & Rust extractors
validates design
Python extractor stays thin by design; Rust's workspace-crate resolver independently converges with monokl's own.
11 · Python code-intelligence landscape
tree-sitter-python confirmed
Ruff's Rust-native parser crates are a dead end (explicitly unstable). Target Structural precision, not Exact.
12 · Rust throughput, syn, Salsa, tokenizer
keep ra_ap_syntax
syn's fail-fast parsing would blank out symbols on any file with a syntax error — a real regression, not a theoretical one.
13 · Go as language #4
native parser exists
gosyn is real and viable — the strongest native-parser candidate found across every language evaluated this session.
14 · Java as language #5

No native Rust parser exists, but Lombok/Spring prevalence justifies the same investment codegraph made.
01

codegraph, verified

mixed evidence

The architecture holds up under a full source read: tree-sitter parses 20+ languages into a genuine SQLite+FTS5 graph through a deterministic ExtractionOrchestrator → ReferenceResolver → GraphTraverser → ContextBuilder pipeline, exposed to agents mainly through one consolidated MCP tool. That single-tool decision is partly evidence-based — a documented, self-critical experiment showed low-salience steering (tool descriptions, init instructions) reliably failed to change agent behavior and even regressed wall-clock time — but the core premise, "one tool beats many," has no published methodology behind it anywhere. It's a validated negative result wearing a positive-sounding conclusion.

The number that mattered most: an independent third-party replication on the Hono repo found codegraph's published −35% cost-savings claim reversed to a +6.8% cost increase, even though tool-call, token, and latency reductions moved in the claimed direction. Fewer, fresher, uncached tokens per call can cost more than many calls of mostly-cached ones — a mechanism confirmed later in thread 05 from codegraph's own internal data.

Reading the actual source turned up the real weak point, in codegraph's own words: its reference resolver is a confidence-ranked heuristic cascade — over 20 hardcoded per-framework resolvers, with real import-graph parsing as its most precise tier and fuzzy name-matching below that — and its code comments frame this as the project's biggest accumulated technical debt. It has also visibly hit and fixed real scale problems: a WASM/V8 out-of-memory crash on a 137,699-file repo, and it shipped indexing 93% node_modules noise by default before being patched. That's genuine large-codebase battle scarring monokl's design hasn't undergone yet.

Sources
  • colbymchenry/codegraph — cloned source, src/extraction, src/db/schema.sql, src/resolution, src/graph/traversal.ts, src/mcp/tools.ts
  • Adversarially-verified deep-research pass, 95 sub-agents — Hono-repo cost-replication finding
02

oxc_semantic & ra_ap_hir for real resolution

adopt (TS/JS half)

Monokl's spec resolves symbol usage — "find all references," "find the canonical declaration" — with regex and text scanning on top of AST-derived import bindings, not real scope-aware binding. That's precisely the class of heuristic codegraph's own maintainers called their worst debt. Since monokl already parses with OXC and ra-ap-syntax, the question was whether their semantic-analysis siblings close that gap for free.

0.140.0oxc_semantic, lockstep with oxc_parser
14exact-pinned ra_ap_* crates in cargo-modules
~5s / 100crates just for rust-analyzer project load

For TypeScript/JavaScript, oxc_semantic is a clear adopt. It versions in lockstep with the rest of the OXC family already in the dependency tree, consumes the same arena as parsing, and SemanticBuilder::build() yields real scope-aware binding — shadowing, hoisting, TDZ, redeclaration — for a single additional linear traversal. It's file-scoped, so it doesn't replace oxc_resolver for cross-file specifier resolution; it upgrades what feeds into that combination.

For Rust, ra_ap_hir is real (genuine name resolution, even type inference) and demonstrably embeddable — cargo-modules proves it — but it wants a populated HirDatabase via cargo metadata and crate-graph construction, a cost rust-analyzer's own maintainers peg at roughly five seconds per hundred crates just waiting on rustc. That's a warm-server cost model, not a cold-CLI one. It only becomes practical if monokl grows a persistent process — which is exactly what thread 07 evaluates independently.

Sources
  • docs.rs/oxc_semantic · github.com/oxc-project/oxc
  • github.com/regexident/cargo-modules — real ra_ap_* embedding precedent
  • rust-lang/rust-analyzer#17491 — project-load cost
03

Ranking beyond BM25

adopt narrowly

Aider's repo map is, read straight from source, literally networkx.pagerank() over a tree-sitter-derived def/ref graph, with hand-tuned edge-weight multipliers and a binary search to hit a token budget. It's well engineered — and completely unvalidated. No benchmark anywhere compares it to plain grep, BM25, or random selection; it's justified by analogy to PageRank's success on the web, not by code-retrieval evidence.

Hybrid lexical+semantic retrieval is a genuinely mixed picture, not a trend to chase: Sourcegraph Cody actually moved away from embeddings back to native code search, citing scaling and cost. The pattern that holds across every tool surveyed is sharper than any single claim — embedding rerank shows up only in products with server-side vector-DB infrastructure. No local-first CLI tool runs it by default. That's real signal for what monokl should stay away from, not just an absence of counter-evidence.

SQLite FTS5 hardcodes k1=1.2, b=0.75 — not tunable. codegraph is stuck with generic-prose defaults no matter what it wants. Monokl's custom BM25 with B=0.5 is at least positioned to do better for code's more length-uniform "documents" — though no rigorous published research validates that tuning either. This is folklore territory across the whole field, not a solved problem anyone is hiding.

Recommendation: adopt explicit over-fetch-then-rerank staging — the one pattern with real cross-tool evidence (Continue.dev, codegraph, general two-stage IR). A small import-proximity nudge is defensible as a minor multiplier. Do not build Aider-style graph ranking as a primary driver, and do not add embedding rerank by default.

Sources
  • Aider-AI/aider — repomap.py
  • sourcegraph.com — how Cody understands your codebase
  • arXiv:2406.14497 — CodeRAG-Bench
  • sqlite.org/fts5.html
04

How agents actually query

grammar confirmed

Every purpose-built lexical tool surveyed — Claude Code's Grep, Cline, Continue.dev, GitHub's MCP search_code — uses regex or qualifier syntax. Natural language shows up only as a separate, explicitly-labeled tool (Sourcegraph's nls_search, Cursor's semantic search), never as freeform input mixed into a grep-style tool. That's a cross-vendor pattern, not a guess, and it's the closest thing to direct validation monokl's +/-/"phrase"/regex: grammar gets.

Real trajectory data adds texture: Anthropic's own production logs found agents "default to overly long, specific queries that return few results" — and fixed it by editing the tool description, not the grammar. Two 2026 papers independently found grep/keyword agentic search matches or beats vector retrieval, which is direct support for monokl's text-prefilter-first pipeline overall.

Recommendation: keep the grammar as-is. Add concrete before/after query examples to the tool's parameter description — Anthropic's proven fix pattern — and add a tolerant natural-language fallback: detect question-like input (where/how/?, five-plus words, no modifiers) and degrade gracefully to bare-optional-term matching instead of erroring.

Sources
  • anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents
  • anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system
  • cursor.com/docs/agent/tools/search
  • arXiv:2605.15184 · arXiv:2602.23368 — grep vs. vector retrieval
05

Eval harness methodology

build it

codegraph actually runs two harnesses people conflate: a 12-case unit-style recall/MRR check, and a real headless-agent A/B system in scripts/agent-eval/. Reading the A/B system's own docs turns up why its cost numbers didn't survive replication — and it half-confesses this itself. Its flagship benchmark table is one run per arm by design, explicitly flagged as "a snapshot — run-to-run variance is real." That same single-run data already shows the with-tokens-down/cost-up pattern the outside replication later confirmed independently.

The mechanism, in codegraph's own analysis: the baseline arm's huge token volume is mostly cheap cached re-reads (~$0.10–0.30/MTok) of files already seen; the tool-assisted arm's payloads are fresh, uncached, full-price input. Fewer calls with more fresh tokens can cost more than many calls of mostly-cached ones. Separately, a silent SDK field-semantics change — result.usage switching from cumulative to last-turn-only — quietly corrupted an earlier published "−34% tokens" figure; the real number was closer to 90%.

Proposed v1 for monokl, buildable now: two layers, not one. A cheap, deterministic retrieval eval (RepoBench-R or CodeSearchNet style, recall@k/MRR) run on every commit, plus a properly-powered agent A/B — model and effort pinned and logged, minimum five runs per condition reporting median and IQR, ≥10 repos with a task list frozen before either arm runs. Report token and dollar deltas separately, broken out by cache-read vs. fresh-input mix, so a token win is never presented as a cost win without that caveat.

Sources
  • codegraph — scripts/agent-eval/run-all.sh, docs/benchmarks/codegraph-ab-matrix.md, call-sequence-analysis.md
  • arXiv:2306.03091 — RepoBench · arXiv:1909.09436 — CodeSearchNet
06

Scale & memory targets, checked against real numbers

mostly generous
296 MB/sOXC single-thread parse, M3 Max
2.0 GB/sripgrep literal scan
90–140 MBWorkspaceIndex @ 50k files
4–8×smaller than the abandoned trigram index

OXC's own benchmark suite gives real, reproducible numbers: 296 MB/s single-threaded on an M3 Max, roughly 3.4× swc and 5.3× biome — matching OXC's own marketing claim almost exactly, for once. ripgrep's published benchmarks show ~2 GB/s literal scanning and a 75,000-file Linux-kernel-scale walk completing in 82ms. Against those, monokl's <15s cold-build target at 50k files has enormous headroom for TypeScript/JavaScript — a realistic ~5KB average file size puts the pure parse well under a second even single-threaded.

The back-of-envelope memory arithmetic (FxHashMap overhead, String heap cost, Vec growth factor, all shown in the work) lands the WorkspaceIndex at roughly 90–140MB at 50k files and 190–270MB at 100k — SymbolIndex dominates at ~80% of that. Even at the pessimistic end, that's 4–8× smaller than the 600MB–1.2GB the spec's own abandoned trigram index measured. The rejection of that design was justified, not marginal.

The real gap: no published throughput number exists for ra_ap_syntax parsing alone. Every available rust-analyzer number measures full semantic analysis — crate resolution, macro expansion, trait solving — not comparable to monokl's syntax-only path. Monokl's Rust-side latency targets are currently unvalidated in either direction. Filling in the spec's own already-stubbed benches/pipeline.rs criterion groups is the cheap fix, not more estimation.

Sources
  • oxc-project/bench-javascript-parser-written-in-rust
  • ripgrep.dev/benchmarks
  • ntietz.com — Rust HashMap overhead
07

Persistent session vs. cold start

keep stateless

This thread caught a bad citation before it could calcify: the "codegraph went from 25 minutes to under a minute" anecdote used to frame this question turned out, on checking against codegraph's actual release notes, to be a SQLite WAL/journal I/O fix specific to slow or throttled disks — the release notes say outright "no change occurs on fast disks." It doesn't transfer to the stateless-vs-daemon question at all.

The honest finding underneath: nobody has measured this, including monokl itself. The spec's own benches/pipeline.rs has four criterion groups still sitting as empty stubs. Reasoning from adjacent measured numbers, the fold step — re-aggregating already-parsed per-file data into ImportGraph/SymbolIndex on a fresh CLI process, not re-parsing — lands at roughly 100–500ms at 10k files and 300ms–1.5s at 50k, a small fraction of the 15s cold-build budget.

A third middle-ground option — snapshotting the built WorkspaceIndex to disk instead of a full daemon — turns out to fight the spec's own intentions: FileIdx is deliberately non-Serialize, described in the spec itself as "a compile-time guard against leaking across rebuild boundaries." Snapshotting would mean loosening a safety invariant that was added on purpose.

Recommendation: keep the current stateless design at ≤50k files — the fold cost is modest next to LLM think-time per round trip, and monokl already rejected one stateful design (the trigram index) for memory cost once already. An optional daemon mode is worth building only for 100k+-file monorepos, and only after the stubbed benchmarks replace this estimate with real numbers.

Sources
  • arXiv:2405.15793 · codegraph releases — v1.4.0 notes
  • monokl spec, local — benches/pipeline.rs stub groups, FileIdx non-Serialize rationale
08

Parallel-parse commit ordering

no change needed

Answered directly from the spec, no new research required. codegraph needs strict sequential commit order because its heuristic resolver disambiguates same-named candidates by database insertion order — a workaround for not having real import resolution. Monokl's WorkspaceIndex::build runs parallel analysis via rayon, then sorts by source_path after completion — order-independent by construction, because oxc_resolver and resolve_rust_path resolve each import to a specific file deterministically. There's no name-based candidate list anywhere in the design that needs an arbitrary tie-break.

Everywhere multiple candidates genuinely can occur — SymbolIndex::lookup, definition's re-export ranking — the spec already sorts on explicit keys (path, line, re-export flag), not insertion order. Monokl sidesteps the problem codegraph built a bounded-window, strictly-ordered flush pipeline to solve. Worth one line in the spec as a design note, so a future contributor doesn't "fix" a bug that isn't there.

09

Was Rust & Python actually covered?

gap, now closed

A fair question stopped this dossier mid-stream: threads 01–08 were implicitly TypeScript/JS-heavy. Rust got real attention in two places — thread 02 found ra_ap_hir needs a warm daemon to be practical, and thread 06 found zero published throughput number exists for ra_ap_syntax parse-only performance — both flagged gaps, not filled ones. Python got essentially nothing, which tracks with the spec's own honesty that it's unimplemented, forward-looking-only work (Part 4 §3). Three follow-on threads below close that.

10

codegraph's Python & Rust extractors, read in full

validates design

codegraph's Python extractor is genuinely thin — 53 lines against Rust's 152 — with only four hand-written hooks (type-hint signatures, async detection, a purely textual @staticmethod check rather than real decorator resolution, and import mapping). No dedicated __all__ handling, no real decorator resolution, no dunder-method special-casing — all of it falls to the generic tree-walking engine. The implicit rationale: Python's grammar is structurally regular enough that hand-tuning barely pays for itself. That's a reasonable precedent for monokl's own future Python analyzer to lean generic-first rather than front-load logic the way the TS analyzer does.

Rust's extractor is comparably sophisticated to TypeScript's — real handling for chained-builder return-type normalization, impl/impl Trait for X receiver-type resolution including generics, recursive use-path unwrapping. But it has zero lifetime handling and zero macro modeling — macro_rules!/macro_invocation appear nowhere in its type lists. Even a mature, production, issue-hardened tool just punts on Rust macros entirely.

Independent convergent validation: codegraph's cargo-workspace.ts resolves cross-crate use crate_name::... paths via a workspace package-root map — the same concept monokl's spec already has (resolve_rust_path + package_roots), arrived at separately. Good sign the existing design there is sound, not a coincidence worth second-guessing.
Sources
  • codegraph — src/extraction/languages/python.ts (53 lines), rust.ts (152 lines), src/resolution/frameworks/python.ts, rust.ts, cargo-workspace.ts
11

Python code-intelligence landscape

tree-sitter-python confirmed

The tempting Rust-native alternative to tree-sitter-python turned out to be a dead end: Ruff's own ruff_python_ast/ruff_python_parser crates are explicitly disclaimed by Ruff itself as unstable internal implementation details — still v0.0.x, "frequent breaking changes" in their own words. Not a publishable dependency contract. tree-sitter-python's actual open issues cluster around bleeding-edge type-hint syntax (PEP 604/695 unions and type aliases) — not the decorators, classes, and __all__ handling monokl's Part 4 §3 questions actually need, which sit on stable ground.

Telling data point: Sourcegraph's own precision-focused Python tool, scip-python, is a fork of pyright — not a lighter structural analyzer built in-house. Even a well-resourced team reached for the full type checker rather than approximate it. That's good validation that Structural precision (not Exact) is the pragmatic, well-precedented v1.1 target, not corner-cutting.

Pyright resolves __all__ and re-exports at the binder phase, before type inference — genuinely cheap, syntax-level work, directly supporting Structural-tier implementation of two of the spec's six open Python questions without a type checker. Separately: monokl's existing tokenizer needs no changes for Python — snake_case already segments correctly on the existing _ delimiter rule; the @ decorator gap is a symbol-schema problem (a decorator field, already floated in the spec), not a tokenizer problem.

Caught a real spec bug in passing: a reference to CapabilityPrecision::Approximate, which isn't an actual variant of the real enum (Unsupported < Heuristic < Structural < Exact). Fixed in the spec to read Heuristic.
Sources
  • tree-sitter/tree-sitter-python · Jedi docs · pyright binder source
  • Ruff crate READMEs (github.com/astral-sh/ruff) — instability disclaimers
12

Rust: throughput, syn, Salsa, tokenizer

keep ra_ap_syntax

No published ra_ap_syntax parse-only throughput exists anywhere, confirmed harder this round — rust-analyzer's own crates/syntax doesn't even have a benches/ directory. Reasoning from adjacent data points (rowan reported ~2× slower than syntree for tree construction alone; tree-sitter-rust, a comparably lossless parser, runs ~3× slower than rustc's hand-written parser), a defensible bound is low tens of MB/s — plausibly 3–10× slower than syn.

Why that cost is probably worth paying: syn::File::parse fails fast — it returns Err at the first bad token with no partial-parse mode, the documented pattern being to emit compile_error! and stop. ra_ap_syntax is IDE-designed to always produce a tree, tagging error nodes instead of aborting. Monokl searches real working trees — WIP branches, merge-conflict markers, mid-edit files. A single syntax error anywhere in a .rs file would make syn yield zero symbols for that entire file. That's a real regression, not a theoretical one — the unquantified throughput cost of keeping ra_ap_syntax is the better trade.

A genuinely new option surfaced: Salsa, rust-analyzer's incremental-computation engine, is architecturally independent of ra_ap_hir — it has real standalone precedent (Astral's ty Python type checker and Biome's analyzer layer both use it decoupled from rust-analyzer's own queries). Monokl could define its own memoized queries — symbols-for-file, postings-for-term — without ever loading a crate graph via cargo metadata. A materially lighter middle ground than thread 07's daemon-or-nothing framing, worth its own investigation track independent of the ra_ap_hir decision.

Tokenizer check, traced against the actual code: macro invocations, turbofish, and derive-attribute contents all tokenize sensibly, contrary to worry. Two real gaps: short lifetimes ('a) are dropped as noise by the length filter, and STOP_WORDS omits crate, self, super, dyn, async, await, unsafe — near-universal tokens across any Rust corpus, free precision left on the table. Fixed directly in the spec — all seven now added to the verbatim STOP_WORDS constant.

Sources
  • rust-lang/rust-analyzer#17491 — "twice as slow as syntree"
  • docs.rs/syn — parse::Error
  • Astral's ty / red-knot — standalone Salsa precedent
13

Go as language #4

native parser exists

Go broke the pattern the other three languages set. gosyn (chikaku/gosyn) is real and viable: 152,000+ downloads, weekly commits, MIT-licensed, and — checked directly against source — confirmed Go 1.18+ generics support (parse_type_parameters, generic instantiation/pointer types both present in source and tests). This is the strongest native-parser candidate found across every language evaluated this session; unlike Python and Java, Go didn't need to fall back to tree-sitter at all.

152k+gosyn downloads
3m26scold go/packages.Load on a 20k-package monorepo
105lines of codegraph's hand-tuned go.ts extractor

Real semantic analysis is daemon-only by the same argument as ra_ap_hir: a 20k-package monorepo took 3m26s cold to load via go/packages.Load, and even a warm gopls daemon took 10+ seconds to serve a new client on a 2,047-package repo. But import resolution is genuinely easier than Rust's for the common case — no macros, no monomorphization — and codegraph's own resolveGoCrossPackageReference proves a go.mod-module-directive-plus-path-stripping heuristic works today. Two gaps worth scoping out of v1 explicitly: go.work multi-module workspaces (codegraph itself only reads the root go.mod), and //go:build tag-gated files (gopls itself can't auto-detect arbitrary build tags beyond filename convention — expect phantom duplicate symbols across tag-gated variants).

Recommendation: native Structural-tier analyzer via gosyn, heuristic go.mod-based import resolution mirroring resolve_rust_path's shape. Tokenizer needs func, package, chan, defer, select, range, go, iota added to STOP_WORDS when this lands.

Sources
  • chikaku/gosyn
  • golang/go#69523 · golang/go#48829 — package-load cost
  • codegraph — src/extraction/languages/go.ts, resolution/go-module.ts, frameworks/go.ts, frameworks/goframe.ts
14

Java as language #5

tree-sitter, hand-tuned

No viable native Rust Java parser exists — checked oak-java and java-lang specifically, both single-maintainer, pre-1.0, near-zero organic adoption. tree-sitter-java is the correct choice, confirmed decisively by codegraph's own "native, no-WASM" performance kernel: even it compiles tree-sitter-java natively via FFI rather than replacing the grammar.

Java's semantic-analysis field is strictly bimodal — full JDT/javac classpath resolution (daemon-only, with real documented pain: 20s cold completion on multi-million-line projects, OOM crashes importing 3000+-file projects) or pure syntax. Unlike Rust/Go, there's no established lightweight middle tier at all. And unlike Rust/TS/Go, idiomatic Java leans much more heavily on JAR-only external symbols (JDK, Spring, Guava, Lombok) with no local source — the same structural wall every non-JVM tool hits, just harder here.

codegraph's actual Java extractor is 334 lines — more hand-tuned than even its Rust extractor — but roughly 150 of those lines are one feature: Lombok-generated-member synthesis (@Getter/@Data/@Builder → synthetic getters/setters/equals/hashCode), because Lombok codegen would otherwise silently break call-chain resolution. It also has a dedicated Spring resolver (route extraction, config binding, DI convention-matching) — but notably no Maven/Gradle multi-module resolver, a real gap even in a mature production tool.

Recommendation: hand-tuned Structural-tier analyzer on tree-sitter-java, matching the same investment codegraph made — Lombok synthesis is worth it, Maven/Gradle multi-module resolution stays Heuristic, Exact is off the table (daemon-only). Tokenizer needs public, private, protected, static, final, void, implements, package, throws, abstract, instanceof, null added to STOP_WORDS when this lands (new/super already covered).

Sources
  • oak-java · java-lang — both non-viable, checked directly
  • eclipse-jdtls/eclipse.jdt.ls#3202 · #1469
  • codegraph — src/extraction/languages/java.ts (334 lines), resolution/frameworks/java.ts

Also note what domain/field this paper is in (e.g. is it about code search, LLM agents, information retrieval, software engineering tools, etc.) and who the authors/affiliations are if stated.

result.output:
# Paper Summary: Reliable Graph-RAG for Codebases

## Domain & Authors
This paper addresses **Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for software engineering**, specifically repository-level code analysis. The author is Manideep Reddy Chinthareddy, a Software Engineer from Centerville, USA.

## Problem Addressed
The paper tackles a critical limitation in code-based RAG systems: "vector similarity often introduces context flattening" and "fails on multi-hop architectural reasoning." Traditional vector-only retrieval cannot reliably capture structural dependencies like inheritance chains, dependency injection patterns, and interface-driven wiring that are essential for answering complex code questions.

## Methodology
The research compares three retrieval approaches on Java codebases (Shopizer, ThingsBoard, OpenMRS Core):

1. **No-Graph**: Standard vector similarity search over code chunks
2. **LLM-KB**: LLM-generated dependency graphs built during indexing
3. **DKB (Proposed)**: Deterministic AST-derived graphs using Tree-sitter parsing with bidirectional traversal and interface-aware expansion

All approaches use identical 15-question benchmark suites per repository and shared hyperparameters (chunk_size=1000, top-k=10).

## Key Findings

**Indexing Performance:**
- DKB builds graphs in seconds (2.81s on Shopizer; 13.77s on ThingsBoard; 5.60s on OpenMRS)
- LLM-KB requires substantially longer (200.14s, 883.74s, 222.17s respectively)

**Indexing Reliability (Critical Finding):**
- LLM-KB exhibits probabilistic incompleteness: on Shopizer, 377 files were "SKIPPED/MISSED by LLM"
- File success rate: 0.688 (833/1210 files processed)
- Chunk coverage: LLM-KB at 0.641 vs. DKB at 0.902 compared to baseline
- Graph nodes: LLM-KB produced 842 nodes vs. DKB's 1158 nodes

**Cost Analysis:**
- Shopizer end-to-end costs: $0.04 (No-Graph), $0.09 (DKB), $0.79 (LLM-KB)
- Normalized multipliers: ~2.25× for DKB, ~19.75× for LLM-KB
- Larger workloads amplify the difference: on combined OpenMRS+ThingsBoard, LLM-KB reached 45.64× multiplier

**Query Latency:**
- No-Graph: 9.52±2.98s (Shopizer); 10.92±1.43s (ThingsBoard); 11.82±2.79s (OpenMRS)
- DKB: 10.51±4.17s; 11.17±1.97s; 12.21±6.96s
- LLM-KB: 13.36±7.87s; 15.29±4.94s; 11.94±4.88s (higher variance and outliers)

**Answer Correctness (Shopizer 15-question suite):**
- DKB: 15/15 correct (perfect)
- LLM-KB: 13/15 correct (2 partial)
- No-Graph: 6/15 correct (highest hallucination risk)

Across all 45 questions (three repositories): DKB achieved 43/45 correct, LLM-KB 38/45, No-Graph 31/45.

## Main Conclusions

1. **Deterministic advantage**: DKB provides "more reliable grounding than probabilistic extraction, particularly for multi-hop and upstream discovery queries"

2. **Indexing completeness matters**: LLM-KB's file-level extraction omissions create "unpredictable blind spots" that reduce both corpus coverage and graph effectiveness

3. **Cost-effectiveness**: DKB offers a "low-overhead, deterministic structural signal" without LLM-mediated inflation, making it practical for production systems

4. **Trade-offs exist**: While DKB excels on architectural questions requiring multi-hop traversal, vector-only performs competitively on localized questions and some repository types

5. **Architectural grounding**: DKB's bidirectional traversal and interface-consumer expansion particularly improve "upstream discovery" scenarios where controllers/services must be identified through interface implementations

## Recommendations
The authors recommend DKB for "correctness-sensitive tasks (impact analysis, controller discovery, transaction boundary inference)" and emphasize that enterprises should prioritize deterministic structure for stable corpus coverage in repository-level code analysis.

content.text:
This is genuinely strong, independent validation of monokl's core architectural bet — and it comes from a completely different angle than anything we've researched so far.

**The paper**: "Reliable Graph-RAG for Codebases" (Chinthareddy, Jan 2026) compares three retrieval strategies for code RAG on real Java codebases (Shopizer, ThingsBoard, OpenMRS): pure vector similarity ("No-Graph"), LLM-generated dependency graphs ("LLM-KB"), and **deterministic AST-derived graphs via Tree-sitter** ("DKB") — which is architecturally almost exactly what monokl's `WorkspaceIndex` (ImportGraph + SymbolIndex, built from real parser output) already is.

The results land squarely in monokl's favor:

- **LLM-generated graphs are unreliable at the indexing step itself**: on Shopizer, the LLM silently skipped/missed 377 of 1210 files (68.8% success rate) — a completeness failure that compounds into every downstream query.
- **Deterministic AST graphs are dramatically cheaper to build**: 2.81–13.77s vs. 200–884s for LLM-generated graphs — 70–150× faster indexing, and only ~2.25× the cost of no-graph-at-all vs. LLM-KB's 20–45× cost multiplier.
- **Answer correctness favors the deterministic graph decisively**: across all 45 benchmark questions, DKB scored 43/45, LLM-KB 38/45, pure vector similarity only 31/45 — and the gap is largest specifically on multi-hop architectural questions (impact analysis, interface-driven controller/service discovery) — exactly the query shape monokl's `dependents`/`refs`/`definition`/`explain`/`data-flow` commands target.

This directly reinforces the "reject embedding-based rerank" call from thread 03, but from a different, stronger angle: it's not just "no evidence embeddings help," it's "deterministic structural graphs measurably beat both vector-only *and* LLM-extracted graphs on the exact kind of question monokl is built to answer." It's also a nice independent precedent for the eval-harness thread — a real methodology (fixed benchmark questions per repo, indexing time/cost/coverage/correctness as named metrics) monokl's own harness could borrow from.

Let me add this as a citation to the spec.

Before leaning on it further, I want it properly vetted rather than taken at face value — it's a single-author paper (Manideep Reddy Chinthareddy, listed as "Software Engineer, Centerville, USA"), which is unusual for what reads as a fairly polished empirical study, and single-author/non-institutional preprints deserve real scrutiny before being cited as load-bearing evidence for a design decision.

input.description: Research Rust patterns for interface/trait-impl graph indices
input.prompt:
Context: I'm helping design "monokl", a Rust code-search/analysis tool for AI coding agents (spec at /Users/gabe/Projects/monokl/docs/monokl-spec.md — a large doc, don't try to read it all, I'll give you the relevant parts inline below). It has a two-level architecture: per-file `LanguageAnalyzer`s produce owned `FileAnalysis` (symbols/dependencies/exports/code-blocks), and `WorkspaceEnricher`s (currently just `ImportGraphEnricher` and `SymbolIndexEnricher`) fold those per-file analyses into a `WorkspaceIndex` holding an `ImportGraph` (file-level forward/reverse import edges, via `FxHashMap<FileIdx, Vec<FileIdx>>`) and a `SymbolIndex` (`FxHashMap<String, Vec<(FileIdx, usize)>>` mapping symbol name to declaration sites). Both are hand-rolled with `rustc-hash`'s `FxHashMap`, not a graph library. `FileIdx` is a `u32` newtype, deliberately not `Serialize` (compile-time guard against leaking across rebuild boundaries). The whole `WorkspaceIndex` is rebuilt fresh in-memory on every invocation (no persistent on-disk graph) via a 3-phase build: parallel per-file analyze (rayon) → sort by path for determinism → stream `enricher.update()` per file → `enricher.finalize()` per enricher once the file-index is fully populated.

We just found a paper (Chinthareddy, "Reliable Graph-RAG for Codebases," arXiv:2601.08773) showing that a deterministic AST-derived graph with "bidirectional traversal and interface-aware expansion" (i.e., given a query that resolves to an interface/trait, expand results to include known implementors, not just the interface declaration) meaningfully improves multi-hop code-question answering versus a plain import graph or vector retrieval — specifically calling out "upstream discovery scenarios where controllers/services must be identified through interface implementations." Monokl's current spec has NO such structure — `RustStructEntry.trait_impls: Vec<String>` records which traits a struct implements (one direction only), but there is no reverse index ("given trait X, find all structs that implement it") anywhere in the design, and no enricher builds one.

Research and report on:

1. **How does real Rust tooling build a "who implements this trait" reverse index?** Specifically investigate `rust-analyzer` itself (it must have this — "find implementations" is a standard IDE feature; look at how `ra_ap_hir`/`ra_ap_ide` structures this, e.g. is there an `Impls` query or a trait-to-impl map in its salsa database?), `cargo-modules` (already known from prior research to embed `ra_ap_*` crates), and any other Rust static-analysis tool (clippy internals, rustdoc's own "Implementors" section on generated docs — rustdoc definitely builds this reverse mapping for its HTML output, worth checking how). What's the standard approach: a dedicated reverse-index data structure built during a full-workspace pass (like monokl's existing enricher pattern), or something computed lazily per-query?

2. **Would `petgraph` (the standard Rust graph crate) be a better fit than monokl's current hand-rolled `FxHashMap<FileIdx, Vec<FileIdx>>` approach for adding this kind of index, or for the `ImportGraph`/`SymbolIndex` generally?** Check petgraph's actual API (crates.io, docs.rs) for whether it offers meaningful ergonomic/performance wins for this specific shape of problem (sparse directed graphs, needing both forward and reverse traversal, needing serialization-free in-memory-only use) over a hand-rolled `FxHashMap`-based adjacency list — or whether petgraph would just add a dependency and abstraction cost without real benefit here, given monokl's existing pattern already works and is simple. Be honest if the answer is "no compelling reason to switch."

3. **Given codegraph's own `GraphTraverser` (a TypeScript tool we've already deep-dived this session) had real production hardening for exactly this kind of traversal** — explicit `visited`/`enqueued` sets, per-node depth limits, hard result-size caps checked at every add site (not just loop tops), batched neighbor fetches to avoid N+1 patterns, and `impact`-radius logic that explicitly excludes `contains` edges to avoid explosion through sibling members — what's the idiomatic Rust way to implement the equivalent (BFS/DFS with cycle-safety and hard caps) for a new `TraitImplIndex`-style enricher and its traversal? Reference real Rust idioms (e.g. `HashSet`-based visited tracking, `VecDeque`-based BFS, explicit `Result`/`Option` for cap-exceeded signaling vs. silent truncation) rather than generic pseudocode.

4. **Fold in what's already been established this session about Rust best practices** (I'll summarize, you don't need to re-research): michi (a sibling project) enforces no `unwrap`/`expect` in lib code via clippy lints, `cargo-deny`, cognitive-complexity limits, and uses `thiserror` for a single error enum; oxc-react-docgen enforces strict arena-containment discipline (no AST/arena references escape a per-file parse call) and uses `FxHashMap`/`FxHashSet` for hot-path maps, `BTreeMap` for anything serialized to JSON (stable key order), `camino::Utf8Path` everywhere. Given these established conventions, sketch (in prose, not full code) what a new `TraitImplEnricher` + `TraitImplIndex` addition to monokl would look like structurally, consistent with the existing `ImportGraphEnricher`/`SymbolIndexEnricher` pattern and these conventions — what would its `update()`/`finalize()` do, what would the reverse-index data structure be, and how would a `definition`/`refs`-style query consume it for "upstream discovery" (interface → implementors) traversal.

Report back under 800 words, organized markdown, with citations/URLs for external claims, ending with a concrete, scoped recommendation.
