export const meta = {
  name: 'monokl-daemon-architecture-research',
  description: 'Deep multi-agent research into daemon/semantic-backend architecture per language, and how to ingest it without flattening per-language distinctions',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Per-language daemon research', detail: 'one agent per real semantic backend: tsserver/typescript-go, ra_ap_hir+Salsa, Python (pyright/Jedi/Pyrefly/ty), gopls, jdtls, clangd, kotlin-lsp, Metals, C#/Ruby/PHP' },
    { title: 'Cross-cutting architecture', detail: 'LSP-as-client feasibility in Rust, multi-language-server unification precedent, confidence/hallucination-prevention signaling' },
    { title: 'Architecture stress-test', detail: 'adversarial multi-lens critique of the proposed PrecisionUpgrader design against every finding above' },
    { title: 'Synthesis', detail: 'final ingestion-model recommendation: what unifies, what must stay distinct per language, and why' },
  ],
}

const CONTEXT = "You're researching a design question for \"monokl,\" a Rust crate that does AST-aware " +
"semantic code search for AI coding agents. You have no other context from any prior conversation — " +
"everything you need is below. This research feeds a real architectural decision, not a survey for " +
"its own sake — be skeptical, verify real project status/maintenance/docs, and say plainly when " +
"evidence is thin rather than filling gaps with plausible-sounding guesses.\n\n" +
"BACKGROUND: monokl's per-file analyzers (OXC for TS/JS, ra_ap_syntax for Rust, tree-sitter for " +
"Python/Java, gosyn for Go, plus a new generic tree-sitter fallback tier for C/C++/Bash/C#/Ruby/PHP, " +
"plus a new optional Clang-subprocess tier for C/C++ and JVM-subprocess tier for Kotlin/Scala) all " +
"report resolution quality via CapabilityPrecision::{Unsupported, Heuristic, Structural, Exact}. " +
"Real semantic resolution (name/type resolution, cross-file reference correctness) for several " +
"languages needs a REAL compiler/language-server backend with live project state — this is " +
"\"Exact\" tier and has been deliberately deferred as a daemon/session-mode investigation track, " +
"since monokl itself has no daemon by default (every invocation is a fresh process reading from an " +
"on-disk cache, no persistent background service).\n\n" +
"A draft architecture has been proposed for this daemon tier, NOT YET FINAL, which this research " +
"must stress-test: a \"PrecisionUpgrader\" trait, separate from the existing per-file " +
"\"LanguageAnalyzer\" trait, that takes an already-produced result and optionally promotes its " +
"CapabilityPrecision using an external resource (a real compiler/language-server). A \"lifetime\" " +
"field distinguishes how that resource is held: PerCall (spawn fresh, use once, discard — e.g. a " +
"Clang subprocess invoked per query), PerInvocation (constructed once, reused across all files in " +
"one CLI run), and Session (reserved, not yet implemented — held warm across many calls within " +
"whatever process embeds monokl for a while, e.g. a future MCP server or another long-lived host " +
"process). The goal of your research is to find out whether THIS shape survives contact with how " +
"real per-language semantic backends actually work, or whether something about a specific " +
"language's real tooling would force a different, incompatible design.\n\n" +
"monokl's stated priority, verbatim from the person who owns this project: \"The goal is not to " +
"provide the same exact data for all languages but to enable LLMs/agents to understand the code as " +
"it is. In high quality, without errors or omissions which can cause hallucinations or other " +
"issues.\" Read that as a real constraint on your recommendation, not a nice-to-have: don't propose " +
"flattening a language's real semantic richness into a generic lowest-common-denominator shape just " +
"because it's convenient to unify. Where a language's tool exposes something genuinely " +
"language-specific and valuable (e.g. Rust trait resolution, Java's classpath-derived facts, " +
"Kotlin's smart-cast information), say so explicitly and describe how monokl should carry that " +
"without diluting it — a per-language extension structure, not forcing everything through one " +
"generic field set."

const LANGS = [
  { key: 'typescript', prompt: CONTEXT + "\n\n## Your language: TypeScript/JavaScript\n\n" +
"Research the real daemon/semantic-backend landscape for TS/JS, beyond what monokl already has " +
"(OXC's own parser, and oxc_semantic — already adopted, file-scoped scope/symbol resolution with " +
"no cross-file capability).\n\n" +
"1. tsserver — Microsoft's own TypeScript language service, what VS Code and every real TS " +
"tooling integration actually uses for full project-wide type-checking/resolution. Real " +
"architecture: how does it manage project state (tsconfig project graph, incremental " +
"type-checking), what's its real cold-start/warm-start cost model at realistic scale (cite real " +
"numbers if you can find them), and what does it expose as a consumable interface (its own " +
"protocol via typescript-language-server, or the raw tsserver protocol itself)?\n" +
"2. typescript-go (microsoft/typescript-go, the new native Go port of the compiler) — does it " +
"expose its own language-server/daemon mode, and if so, is it meaningfully lighter/faster than " +
"the original tsserver given it's a from-scratch native reimplementation?\n" +
"3. What real semantic facts would an Exact tier actually add over what oxc_semantic already " +
"gives monokl today — cross-file type resolution, generic instantiation, module-augmentation " +
"resolution, overload resolution, inferred expression types.\n" +
"4. Data-quality/confidence question: does tsserver (or typescript-go) ever return a best-guess " +
"answer with no signal that it's uncertain (e.g. ambiguous overload resolution, an any-typed " +
"fallback due to missing type info)? If monokl surfaces a tsserver-derived answer as Exact " +
"precision when tsserver itself silently degraded to a best-effort guess, that's exactly the kind " +
"of overclaiming that could mislead an agent. Find out if there's any way to detect this from the " +
"response shape.\n\n" +
"Output: a verdict on whether the PerCall/PerInvocation/Session lifetime model fits how " +
"tsserver/typescript-go actually need to be run (they're famously stateful, incremental, and " +
"expensive to cold-start — does that force Session-only, or does something lighter suffice?). " +
"Cite real sources. 600-800 words." },

  { key: 'rust', prompt: CONTEXT + "\n\n## Your language: Rust\n\n" +
"Go deep on ra_ap_hir plus Salsa — monokl already has surface-level research on this (the ~5s/100 " +
"crates cargo-metadata-plus-crate-graph cost, the daemon-fits-a-warm-process framing) but needs " +
"real depth on the ARCHITECTURE, not just the cost number.\n\n" +
"1. rust-analyzer's own daemon internals: how it actually manages state across a long-lived " +
"session — its VFS (virtual file system) layer, the Salsa database and how it invalidates/" +
"recomputes on file changes, its GlobalState/world-snapshot model for serving concurrent LSP " +
"requests while background analysis continues. This is the real precedent for what monokl's own " +
"Session lifetime would need to hold.\n" +
"2. What data would monokl actually ingest — real HIR-level facts (resolved paths, trait " +
"resolution including blanket impls and where-clause-gated impls, macro-expanded code visibility, " +
"generic monomorphization info) that go meaningfully beyond ra_ap_syntax's current syntax-only " +
"tier and monokl's own hand-rolled TraitImplIndex. Be specific about what's genuinely new " +
"information vs. a precision upgrade of something monokl already computes heuristically.\n" +
"3. Confidence/uncertainty signaling: does rust-analyzer's HIR layer have any notion of " +
"resolution-failed/ambiguous vs. silently picking one candidate? How does it handle genuinely " +
"ambiguous cases (trait method resolution with multiple candidate impls, macro-generated code it " +
"can't expand)? Does it produce diagnostics for these?\n" +
"4. Real precedent for lighter-than-full-rust-analyzer Salsa usage: Astral's ty (Python type " +
"checker, uses Salsa independently) and Biome — check if either publishes anything about running " +
"Salsa in a shorter-lived/non-daemon way relevant to monokl's PerInvocation tier.\n\n" +
"Output: does rust-analyzer's real architecture fit the proposed PerCall/PerInvocation/Session " +
"model, or does Salsa's incremental-database design mean something in between (e.g. " +
"PerInvocation is where most real value is, since a fresh Salsa db still gets memoization across " +
"all files/queries within one run, even without cross-invocation warmth)? Cite real sources. " +
"600-800 words." },

  { key: 'python', prompt: CONTEXT + "\n\n## Your language: Python\n\n" +
"monokl currently uses tree-sitter-python for structural parsing (chosen over Ruff's unstable " +
"Rust-native crates). Research the REAL semantic-daemon landscape — this may be a more interesting " +
"story than Rust/Java/Kotlin/Scala's JVM/daemon-only pattern, because at least one modern Python " +
"type-checker is itself written in Rust. Verify rather than assume:\n\n" +
"1. Pyrefly (Meta's newer Python type checker — check if this is real, its current status, and " +
"specifically whether it's implemented in Rust) and ty (Astral's Python type checker/language " +
"server, already flagged elsewhere in monokl's research as a real Salsa-based Rust project) — " +
"for each: real project maturity, whether it exposes an LSP/daemon interface, and critically, " +
"whether either could plausibly be used as a Rust-native LIBRARY dependency (not just a " +
"subprocess) given monokl's strong preference for pure-Rust in-process parsing where possible.\n" +
"2. pyright (Microsoft's, TypeScript/Node-hosted, the most feature-complete/widely-used Python " +
"language server) and Jedi (pure Python, lighter-weight, real and mature) — real cost model " +
"(cold-start, memory, whether they need a resolved virtualenv/site-packages to work at all — " +
"Python's version of Java's classpath problem) and what their docs/issues say about degraded " +
"operation when project setup is incomplete.\n" +
"3. What real semantic facts would an Exact tier add over tree-sitter-python's current Heuristic-" +
"tier forward-reference handling (PyCG's own paper reports 99.2% precision/69.9% recall for " +
"dependency-free static call-graph construction) — real type-narrowing, decorator-transformed " +
"signatures, dynamic attribute resolution via __getattr__.\n" +
"4. Confidence/uncertainty signaling: Python's dynamic-typing nature means a lot of real answers " +
"are genuinely uncertain (duck typing, monkey-patching, kwargs-based dispatch). Do any of these " +
"tools expose a confidence or inferred-vs-declared distinction, or do they always return one " +
"best-guess answer?\n\n" +
"Output: is there a real, pure-Rust or at-least-lighter-than-JVM path to Python's Exact tier via " +
"Pyrefly/ty specifically, or does the evidence not support that and Python is stuck with " +
"pyright/Jedi-style subprocess daemons like everyone else? Cite real sources. 600-800 words." },

  { key: 'go', prompt: CONTEXT + "\n\n## Your language: Go\n\n" +
"monokl already has real cold-start numbers for go/packages.Load (3m26s on a 20k-package " +
"monorepo, golang/go#69523) and gopls warm-daemon latency (10+ seconds serving a new client on a " +
"2,047-package repo, golang/go#48829) — don't re-derive these, use them as given.\n\n" +
"1. gopls's real internal architecture — how it holds workspace state (its own view/snapshot " +
"model, how it handles multiple modules/go.work workspaces — already an explicit v1 gap in " +
"monokl's current Go plan), and how its LSP surface is structured.\n" +
"2. What real semantic facts would an Exact tier add over gosyn's current native-Rust Structural-" +
"tier parsing — real type information, interface-satisfaction checking (Go's structural typing " +
"means whether type X implements interface Y is NOT statically declared the way Rust's impl " +
"Trait for Type is — a fundamentally different and harder discovery problem than monokl's " +
"existing TraitImplIndex model, since there's no explicit impl site to index). Dig into how " +
"gopls itself solves interface-satisfaction discovery internally.\n" +
"3. Confidence/uncertainty signaling: does gopls ever return a low-confidence or ambiguous answer " +
"for interface-satisfaction queries (many types could structurally satisfy an interface — how " +
"does it rank/limit these, and does it expose there were multiple candidates)?\n" +
"4. Real precedent check: has anyone published real numbers on running gopls in a shorter-lived " +
"way for one-shot tooling use?\n\n" +
"Output: given the real cold-start numbers already established, does gopls realistically only fit " +
"the Session lifetime, and what does that imply concretely for monokl's Go story? Cite real " +
"sources. 500-700 words." },

  { key: 'java', prompt: CONTEXT + "\n\n## Your language: Java\n\n" +
"monokl already has real numbers for jdtls (20s cold completion on multi-million-line projects, " +
"1-2s warm; OOM crashes importing 3000+-file projects, eclipse-jdtls/eclipse.jdt.ls#3202 and " +
"#1469) — don't re-derive these.\n\n" +
"1. jdtls's real internal architecture — the JDT Core Model it's built on, how it manages " +
"classpath resolution (Maven/Gradle project import, the exact mechanism and why it's expensive), " +
"and its LSP surface shape.\n" +
"2. What real semantic facts would an Exact tier add over tree-sitter-java's current Structural-" +
"tier parsing (already includes hand-tuned Lombok-generated-member synthesis) — real overload " +
"resolution, generic type inference, and resolution of JAR-only external symbols (JDK/Spring/" +
"Guava — already flagged as a structural wall no non-JVM tool can cross). Quantify how much of a " +
"typical real Java codebase's symbol references are external-JAR-only if any published data " +
"exists.\n" +
"3. Confidence/uncertainty signaling: does jdtls/JDT expose any distinction between resolved-with-" +
"full-confidence and best-guess (ambiguous overload resolution, or a missing classpath entry " +
"causing a silent fallback to an unresolved-type placeholder)?\n\n" +
"Output: given jdtls's documented OOM/cold-start pain, is Session the only viable lifetime for " +
"Java too, and specifically does the OOM-on-3000-plus-files problem mean monokl needs a real per-" +
"project-size gate rather than just slow-but-eventually-works? Cite real sources. 500-700 words." },

  { key: 'cpp', prompt: CONTEXT + "\n\n## Your language: C/C++\n\n" +
"monokl already has a proposed optional PerCall tier for C/C++ using clang-ast (subprocess: " +
"clang -Xclang -ast-dump=json -fsyntax-only), chosen over libclang FFI (clang-sys) for lighter " +
"integration friction, plus real findings on -frecovery-ast (RecoveryExpr, real AST preservation " +
"across semantic errors, on by default since Clang 11) and the compilation-database problem " +
"(real graceful degradation in clangd, but missing #includes are still a hard preprocessor-level " +
"failure). Don't re-derive any of this — your job is the DAEMON question specifically:\n\n" +
"1. clangd — the real, mature C/C++ language server. How does its architecture differ from a " +
"bare clang-ast subprocess call per file? Specifically: its background-index feature (does it " +
"maintain a persistent, incrementally-updated index across a whole project, and what does that " +
"cost at realistic scale)? Does clangd need a full compilation database to be useful at all, or " +
"does it degrade the same way documented for bare Clang?\n" +
"2. Is clangd the natural Session tier for C/C++ — does adopting the PerCall clang-ast tier now " +
"set monokl up cleanly to add clangd later as the Session tier, or does clangd's architecture " +
"differ enough (its own protocol extensions beyond standard LSP, background-index storage " +
"format) that it's a genuinely separate integration effort?\n" +
"3. Confidence/uncertainty signaling: does clangd surface where AST recovery happened (can monokl " +
"tell a fully-resolved AST node from a RecoveryExpr placeholder after an error), or is that " +
"distinction invisible once consuming clangd's LSP responses?\n\n" +
"Output: verdict on whether clangd is the right Session-tier answer for C/C++, and whether the " +
"already-decided PerCall tier and a future clangd-based Session tier are architecturally " +
"compatible enough to share one PrecisionUpgrader implementation or need to be two separate " +
"implementations. Cite real sources. 500-700 words." },

  { key: 'kotlin', prompt: CONTEXT + "\n\n## Your language: Kotlin\n\n" +
"monokl already researched Kotlin's compiler-as-library options and found: kotlin-compiler-" +
"embeddable is being abandoned (detekt#8027), and the K2 Analysis API's standalone mode was " +
"explicitly documented by JetBrains as in development and subject to incompatible changes, with " +
"IntelliJ plugin development the only officially supported use case — as of that research. Your " +
"job: check whether this has changed, and specifically research the real daemon/LSP story.\n\n" +
"1. kotlin-lsp (JetBrains' own LSP server for Kotlin, check if this project is real, its current " +
"release/maturity status, and what it's actually built on internally — does it use the same K2 " +
"Analysis API standalone mode already flagged as unstable, or something else?). Verify " +
"thoroughly, don't assume from the name alone.\n" +
"2. Real cost model: classpath/dependency resolution requirements, cold-start numbers if " +
"published anywhere.\n" +
"3. Confidence/uncertainty signaling: Kotlin has real language features that create genuine " +
"ambiguity risk if not signaled properly — smart-casting (type narrowing based on control flow, " +
"which can silently fail to apply), nullable type inference, and extension-function resolution " +
"(which extension function applies can depend on import scope in genuinely ambiguous ways). Does " +
"kotlin-lsp expose any signal when these are ambiguous, or does it always return one answer?\n\n" +
"Output: is there now a real path to a Kotlin daemon/Session tier, or does the earlier unstable-" +
"per-JetBrains-docs finding still hold? If real, what's its realistic lifetime fit? Cite real, " +
"current sources — don't rely on the earlier research's conclusion without re-verifying it's " +
"still accurate. 500-700 words." },

  { key: 'scala', prompt: CONTEXT + "\n\n## Your language: Scala\n\n" +
"monokl already researched Scalameta (mature, Scala 3 support solved since 2021-22, real " +
"production precedent including scalex — Scala code intelligence for coding agents, zero build " +
"server, zero compilation) as a PerCall/PerInvocation-friendly parse-only Structural tier. Your " +
"job is the real DAEMON question specifically: Metals.\n\n" +
"1. Metals — the real, mature Scala language server (built on Scalameta plus Build Server " +
"Protocol, used by VS Code/Metals extension and other editors). Real architecture: how does it " +
"get build information (BSP talking to sbt/Bloop/Mill/Gradle), what's its real cold-start cost " +
"model (does it need a full compile to get real semantic info, unlike Scalameta's parse-only " +
"mode), and what does its LSP surface expose?\n" +
"2. What real semantic facts would Metals add over Scalameta's parse-only tier — real implicit " +
"resolution (Scala's implicit/given mechanism is a major source of where-did-this-value-come-" +
"from questions that parse-only analysis cannot answer), real type inference, macro-expansion " +
"visibility.\n" +
"3. Confidence/uncertainty signaling: implicit/given resolution can be genuinely ambiguous " +
"(multiple implicits in scope, resolved by a real but non-obvious priority/specificity " +
"algorithm) — does Metals expose which implicit was selected and why, or just the end result?\n" +
"4. Does Build Server Protocol (BSP) matter architecturally for monokl — is BSP a second " +
"protocol beyond LSP monokl's daemon tier would need to speak for Scala specifically, or does " +
"Metals abstract that away entirely?\n\n" +
"Output: verdict on Metals as the Scala Session tier — real cost model, what it adds over " +
"Scalameta parse-only, and whether BSP introduces a real protocol-diversity problem for monokl's " +
"daemon architecture. Cite real sources. 500-700 words." },

  { key: 'fallback-langs', prompt: CONTEXT + "\n\n## Your languages: C#, Ruby, PHP (monokl's tree-" +
"sitter fallback-tier languages, no bespoke analyzer aspiration yet — lighter treatment than the " +
"other languages in this research batch is fine, but still real)\n\n" +
"For each of C#, Ruby, and PHP: what's the real, mature language-server/daemon option (C#: " +
"OmniSharp and/or the newer official csharp-ls/Roslyn-based server; Ruby: Solargraph and/or " +
"Sorbet; PHP: Intelephense and/or Psalm/Phan's LSP modes)? For each, briefly: real maturity, " +
"rough cost model, and whether any has a notably different architecture from the typical " +
"language-server pattern (e.g. Sorbet's own custom fast-restart daemon model is known for being " +
"unusually fast to cold-start compared to typical language servers — verify this specifically). " +
"Don't go as deep as the other 8 languages in this batch — establish whether any of these three " +
"has a real daemon story worth prioritizing sooner than expected, or whether they're all a safe " +
"same-pattern-as-everything-else story. 400-500 words total." },
]

const CROSS_CUTTING = [
  { key: 'lsp-client-rust', prompt: CONTEXT + "\n\n## Your research area: is a generic Rust LSP " +
"CLIENT architecture real and viable?\n\n" +
"Nearly every real semantic backend being researched in parallel (tsserver via typescript-" +
"language-server, rust-analyzer, gopls, jdtls, clangd, kotlin-lsp, Metals, OmniSharp, Solargraph, " +
"Intelephense) speaks the Language Server Protocol (LSP) as its primary interface. Instead of a " +
"bespoke PrecisionUpgrader implementation per language, could monokl have ONE generic LSP client " +
"PrecisionUpgrader implementation — JSON-RPC transport, request/response correlation, standard " +
"LSP types — parameterized only by which server binary to spawn and how to detect it, with per-" +
"language logic reduced to config plus response-mapping?\n\n" +
"1. Real Rust crates for BUILDING an LSP client (not a server — most Rust LSP crates, like tower-" +
"lsp, are for building servers, since Rust tools like rust-analyzer/ra_ap_* ARE the servers in " +
"this ecosystem, not clients of others). Check lsp-types (the shared type definitions, direction-" +

<result>## Research: How real semantic tools signal (or fail to signal) uncertainty, and what monokl's PrecisionUpgrader should do about it

**1. Neither LSP nor SCIP have a confidence field — verified directly.** Fetching the LSP 3.17 spec directly: `Location {uri, range}`, `LocationLink {originSelectionRange?, targetUri, targetRange, targetSelectionRange}`, and `ResponseError {code, message, data?}` — no field anywhere expresses confidence, ambiguity, or "multiple candidates considered." Fetching SCIP's actual `scip.proto`: `Relationship {symbol, is_reference, is_implementation, is_type_definition, is_definition}` and `Occurrence {range/typed_range, symbol, symbol_roles, syntax_kind, diagnostics, enclosing_range}` — same result, confirming the earlier SCIP finding and showing LSP is no better. The one structural signal LSP carries *incidentally* rather than by design: `textDocument/definition` and `textDocument/references` are typed to return `Location | Location[] | LocationLink[] | null`. A response with cardinality >1 for a query that implies a single binding is a real, always-present ambiguity signal — but nearly every client discards it by taking `result[0]`.

**2. The common pattern across failure modes: internal degradation signals exist but are deliberately smoothed away before reaching the answer surface.** clangd is the clearest case, confirmed against Clang source: `RecoveryExpr` is a real, grep-able AST marker (`<recovery-expr>(...)`, per `StmtPrinter::VisitRecoveryExpr` and Clang's own AST-dump tests) — but clangd's `FindTarget` logic *deliberately resolves through it* to keep hover/go-to-definition looking normal, per explicit test comments like "no overload matches, but we have recovery-expr with the correct type." The degradation is invisible at the LSP layer by design intent, not oversight. TypeScript shows the same pattern differently: unresolved types collapse into the same `any` as a deliberately-untyped value, with no marker distinguishing "genuinely any" from "inference gave up." jdtls's classpath problems surface on a separate build/project-diagnostics channel rather than tainting the specific hover/definition response that used the broken classpath — a consumer reading only per-symbol answers never sees it. Kotlin and Scala are the informative *exceptions*: both eventually gained real, stable, machine-detectable sentinels precisely because the underlying ambiguity was too dangerous to leave silent — Kotlin's `T!` platform-type notation (documented, kotlinlang.org) and internal `ErrorType`/`ErrorTypeKind` (JetBrains/kotlin source); Scala's `diverging implicit expansion` string (Scala 2) and Scala 3's numbered `E172` "Ambiguous given instances" diagnostic. The pattern: whether a signal survives to the surface is a language-community design choice, not a property monokl can assume — so it must go looking for these sentinels itself rather than trusting a "successful" response.

**3. CHA/RTA/points-to literature gives a real, citable precedent, with one caveat.** The precision ladder is real and graded by cost/soundness tradeoff (Dean, Grove & Chambers, CHA, ECOOP 1995; Bacon & Sweeney, RTA, OOPSLA 1996; Andersen 1994; Steensgaard, POPL 1996), and Bravenboer & Smaragdakis's Doop (OOPSLA 2009) proves this is operational, not just conceptual — it exposes context-sensitivity as a selectable, named parameter, i.e., analysis metadata about which tier produced a result. The closest citable principle for "make the tier explicit rather than pretend uniform confidence" is Livshits et al., "In Defense of Soundiness: A Manifesto" (CACM 58(2), 2015): document unsound design choices rather than hide them. Note this is about design-time disclosure, not literal per-fact provenance tagging — applying it to per-fact granularity is our extrapolation, not an existing paper's claim.

**Actionable rules for monokl's PrecisionUpgrader:**
1. Treat response cardinality as a signal: `definition`/`references` returning >1 location for an ostensibly-unambiguous query → downgrade to `Structural`, emit a `Diagnostic` listing all candidates instead of silently taking `[0]`.
2. Maintain a per-backend sentinel table checked against *raw* diagnostics/type-strings, not the polished LSP layer: `<recovery-expr>`/dependent-type markers for Clang; `T!`/`ErrorType`/`ErrorTypeKind` or smart-cast diagnostic IDs for Kotlin; `E172`/"diverging implicit expansion" for Scala; co-occurring unresolved-import diagnostics on an `any`-typed hover for TS.
3. Cross-check project/build-level diagnostics each call (classpath, missing deps) — don't trust a clean per-symbol answer if the file's classpath is known-incomplete.
4. Classify by question type, not tool: closed-world nominal resolution with a language-guaranteed unique answer (Rust trait dispatch post-coherence, Java overload resolution) can earn `Exact`; open-world/coincidental-match questions (Go interface-implementer search, Kotlin extension resolution, C++ ADL with multiple viable candidates) cap at `Structural` even on compiler success, with the full candidate set attached as a `Diagnostic` rather than the tie-broken pick presented alone.
5. Never infer trust from response *shape* alone — since no protocol here carries confidence, silence from LSP/SCIP is absence of evidence, not evidence of correctness.

<result>## Research Findings: Multi-Backend Semantic Data Unification — Precedent Analysis

I verified primary sources directly (SCIP's actual protobuf schema, its design doc, CodeQL's real repo structure, rust-analyzer's documented LSP extensions) rather than relying on recalled summaries. One caveat up front: the shared web-search budget for this session was exhausted before I could run search queries, so everything below comes from direct WebFetch of primary documents, plus one narrative point I flag explicitly as unverified this session.

**1. Sourcegraph (LSIF → SCIP): unifies the reference graph, not the semantics.**
SCIP's own `scip.proto` and `docs/DESIGN.md` (github.com/sourcegraph/scip) show a deliberately narrow common core: a `Relationship` message with four boolean flags (`is_reference`, `is_implementation`, `is_type_definition`, `is_definition`) and an `Occurrence`/`SymbolInformation` pair keyed by a human-readable symbol string. That core generalizes honestly across languages because "X references/implements/defines Y" means roughly the same thing everywhere. Critically, SCIP does *not* try to unify deeper semantics. Its two real extension points are (a) `SymbolInformation.kind`, an enum that keeps growing per-language (`AbstractMethod` for Java/Kotlin, `Accessor` for Ruby, `Contract`/`Modifier` for Solidity) rather than staying generic, and (b) `documentation`/`Signature.language`, which are markdown/text blobs — meaning anything genuinely rich (a Rust trait bound, a Java checked-exception spec) degrades to unstructured prose, not structured data. DESIGN.md is explicit that indexers themselves stay per-language ("tooling for a language tends to be implemented in the same language... impractical to expect indexers to settle on a common implementation"), i.e., unification happens only at the wire format, never in the analysis itself. ## 1. Sourcegraph: LSIF → SCIP was a wire-format fix, not a semantic-unification fix

The LSIF→SCIP rewrite is often assumed to be about reconciling different languages' semantics. It wasn't. Sourcegraph's own SCIP announcement lists the actual drivers: LSIF's "heavy usage of opaque ID numbers to encode the graph structure" made it hard to debug and hard to index incrementally, it has no machine-readable schema ("LSIF doesn't come with a machine-readable schema, and the dynamic graph structure makes it difficult to encode LSIF payloads as a simple set of structs or classes"), and it was slow to produce/consume at scale. SCIP fixed this with human-readable string symbol IDs over Protobuf, yielding measurable wins (e.g. a 10x CI speedup for TypeScript indexing). None of this is about Rust traits vs. Java classpaths — it's encoding engineering (docs.sourcegraph.com / lsif.dev / sourcegraph.com/blog/announcing-scip).

The actual answer to "how do they preserve per-language richness" lives one level down, in SCIP's schema itself (github.com/sourcegraph/scip, scip.proto): a single shared envelope (`Document`, `SymbolInformation`, `Occurrence`, `Relationship`) is used for every language, but the leaf fields are deliberately *not* flattened. `SymbolInformation.kind` is one enum, yet it explicitly enumerates dozens of language-tailored variants rather than one generic "callable": `AbstractMethod` ("for Java, Kotlin etc."), `PureVirtualMethod` ("analogous to AbstractMethod, for C++"), `Accessor`/`MethodAlias`/`SingletonClass` (Ruby-specific), `Contract`/`Modifier` (Solidity-specific). The spec's own rationale: "kind provides a fine-grained category of a symbol, suitable for presenting information about the symbol's meaning in the language... A Java method would have the kind `Method` while a Go function would have the kind `Function`, even if the symbols for these use the same syntax for the descriptor." That's a mature, production system explicitly rejecting lowest-common-denominator collapse in favor of typed per-language leaves inside a shared structural envelope. `Document.language` is likewise a free string, not a closed enum, so new languages don't require a schema break.

## 2. LSP / VS Code: shared baseline + namespaced, gracefully-ignorable extensions

The LSP spec's own extension mechanism is the cleanest precedent for daemon-tier "upgrade" data specifically. It defines a small generic baseline (hover, go-to-def, references, completions, diagnostics — ~18 features) via `vscode.languages.*`, but explicitly reserves a namespace for anything a specific server needs beyond that: methods starting with `$/` (or vendor-prefixed custom methods) are "protocol implementation dependent and might not be implementable in all clients or servers," and a client/server that doesn't support one must simply return `MethodNotFound`. More importantly, the spec's general compatibility rule is: "Clients should ignore server capabilities they don't understand," and enum values are versioned so "the using side of an enumeration shouldn't fail on a value it doesn't know — it should simply ignore it." This is exactly the shape needed when a capability (like a daemon backend) may or may not be present: absence degrades silently instead of breaking the contract.

Semantic tokens push this further with an explicit subtyping model: providers are "free to define new types and modifiers and create a subtype of the standard types," and by declaring the standard type as a supertype, "theme styling rules for `type` will also apply to `templateType`" — i.e., a language-specific extension gets automatic, safe fallback behavior from consumers that only understand the base concept. (code.visualstudio.com/api/language-extensions/semantic-highlight-guide; microsoft.github.io LSP 3.17 spec.)

## 3. CodeQL: literally one schema per language over a shared abstract base

This is the strongest direct match. CodeQL's own repository has a `shared/` tree of "shared, language-agnostic CodeQL libraries" (github.com/github/codeql/tree/main/shared) — `dataflow`, `ssa`, `typetracking`, `typeinference`, `controlflow`, `concepts`, `namebinding`, `util`, etc. — each an abstract framework (QL's module/signature system) that per-language libraries (Java, C++, Python, JS, C#, Go, Ruby, Swift, and now Rust) implement concretely. The Java guide confirms the per-language side: `java.qll` "imports all the core Java library modules" specific to Java/Kotlin (its own AST, call-graph, and metrics classes), which sit on top of, not instead of, the shared dataflow/SSA frameworks. This is a decade-plus-refined, production security-scanning system explicitly choosing "shared base predicates + one full schema per language" over a universal schema — directly validating the research question's hypothesis.

## Recommendation for monokl

All three precedents converge on the same shape monokl's `FileAnalysis`/`LangData` enum already has: shared envelope, per-language typed payload, never a generic fact-soup. Keep it — SCIP's `kind` enum and CodeQL's per-language libraries both show that typed, enumerable per-language richness (Rust trait relations, Java classpath facts, Kotlin smart-casts) survives better as real per-language variants than as generic key/value bags.

But daemon-tier data is structurally different from what `LangData` already models: it's an optional, resource-gated *enrichment pass* over an already-complete base result, produced independently of and later than the base analyzer — not a peer data source. None of the three precedents has an "upgrade pass" concept natively (SCIP documents, CodeQL databases, and LSP capability sets are each produced once, in one pass). The transferable mechanism for *that* specific shape is LSP's capability-negotiation/namespaced-extension pattern: model `PrecisionUpgrader` output as an additive, per-language-typed extension attached alongside the base `LangData` payload (e.g. `daemon_extension: Option<DaemonExtension>` with `DaemonExtension::Rust(RustTraitFacts) | Java(ClasspathFacts) | Kotlin(SmartCastFacts) | ...`), never merged into or replacing the base variant. This gives three properties for free, matching the cited precedents directly: (1) total absence is safe and silent when no upgrader ran or `Session` lifetime isn't available yet — mirroring "clients should ignore capabilities they don't understand"; (2) each language's extension can carry its real, richly-typed semantic facts without warping a shared schema, mirroring CodeQL's independently-versioned per-language packs over a shared base; (3) it stays orthogonal to `PerCall`/`PerInvocation`/`Session` lifetime — which resource produced the upgrade is provenance metadata on the extension, not a structural fork, the same way LSP capability metadata records what a server supports without changing the protocol's shape.

### 1. LSP has no confidence channel — confirmed by direct inspection of the spec

I read the LSP 3.17 spec's response types directly. `Location` carries only `uri`/`range`. `LocationLink` adds `originSelectionRange`/`targetRange`/`targetSelectionRange` — purely positional, nothing epistemic. `ResponseError` carries only `code`/`message`/`data`. There is no field anywhere in `textDocument/definition`, `textDocument/references`, or `textDocument/hover` for "I picked one of several candidates" or "I'm not confident." A server that resolved unambiguously and a server that guessed produce byte-identical response shapes. This matches the prior SCIP finding — I independently re-checked `scip.proto`'s `Relationship` and `Occurrence` messages and confirmed neither has a confidence/approximation field either. **LSP is not better than SCIP here; both protocols simply have no concept of graded confidence.** This is a real, structural gap in the wire format monokl's daemon tier will be talking to, not an oversight monokl can query around.

### 2. The compilers themselves often *do* know — the protocol is what throws it away

This is the important nuance, and it changes the design recommendation. I verified two concrete cases where the underlying resolver internally tracks degradation, but the signal dies before it reaches LSP:

- **Clang/clangd**: `RecoveryExpr` is a real, documented AST node clang emits when it can't resolve an overload, call, or type — it "acts as a placeholder to maintain the rough structure of the parsing tree... but [has] no language semantics attached," often carrying a dependent/placeholder type (LLVM Internals Manual, RecoveryAST section). The compiler *knows* this expression is unresolved. But nothing in `textDocument/hover`'s response schema flags it as such — clangd just emits whatever type string it has.
- **Eclipse JDT**: I pulled the actual source of `IBinding.java` from `eclipse-jdt/eclipse.jdt.core`. `isRecovered()`'s javadoc: *"Return whether this binding is created because the bindings recovery is enabled. This binding is considered to be incomplete."* This is a real, queryable flag JDT sets internally whenever classpath gaps or unresolved types force it to fabricate a placeholder binding — exactly the jdtls classpath-fallback failure mode. It exists on JDT's own DOM API, not on anything jdtls exposes through LSP.
- **TypeScript**: per the TS FAQ (issue #54414 discussion), the checker internally distinguishes a genuine `any` from an unresolved/error type, but the language service collapses both to the string `"any"` in hover output — the wire-level answer is indistinguishable from a deliberate `any`.

The common pattern across these plus Go's structural-satisfaction guessing, Kotlin's smart-cast reversion/platform types, and Scala's implicit-ambiguity resolution: **each resolver has an internal escape-hatch representation for "I couldn't really solve this"** (a top/dependent type, a recovered-binding flag, a platform-type marker, a first-candidate pick), and in every case that escape hatch is a small, enumerable, tool-specific sentinel — not a diagnostic that generically propagates through LSP. That enumerability is what makes generic detection possible: monokl doesn't need per-language semantic understanding, it needs a per-backend denylist of sentinel shapes.

### 3. Precedent from call-graph/points-to literature

The CHA → RTA → points-to (Andersen/Steensgaard) hierarchy is the closest existing precedent for "graded trust in a static answer," and its actual discipline (Grove & Chambers, *A Framework for Call Graph Construction Algorithms*, TOPLAS 2001; Bacon & Sweeney, OOPSLA 1996) is not a magic confidence score — it's that **the analysis tier itself is carried as metadata and never erased**. An edge computed by CHA is never silently reported as if RTA or points-to had produced it; consumers reason differently about a CHA-derived reachability edge than a points-to-derived alias fact. The generalizable rule: precision must be tagged at the source and preserved end-to-end, not inferred after the fact from "did a real tool answer."

### Actionable rules for `PrecisionUpgrader`

1. **A missing `ResponseError` proves nothing.** LSP has no failure mode for "resolved to a degraded fallback" — only for outright request failures. Silence ≠ confidence.
2. **Prefer native/extended APIs over plain LSP** where the backend has one that exposes its own confidence bit (JDT DOM `isRecovered()`, TS `ts.Program`/checker, clangd AST dump) — plain LSP structurally cannot carry the signal even when the compiler computed it.
3. **Maintain a per-backend sentinel denylist** and check every upgrade against it before promoting to `Exact`: JDT `isRecovered()==true`; Clang/clangd dependent/recovery type strings or nonzero diagnostics at the queried span; TS hover text of `any`/`error` not matching an explicit source annotation (diff against OXC's own Heuristic-tier read of the source); Kotlin platform-type markers (`T!`); Scala diverging/ambiguous-implicit compiler notices.
4. **When only generic LSP is available and no sentinel exists**, cap at `Structural` if the file has any diagnostic at or upstream of the queried location, and emit a monokl `Diagnostic` explaining the downgrade — mirroring the CHA discipline of never letting an unsound upstream step silently masquerade as full precision downstream.
5. **Tag every `Exact` result with which backend/operation produced it** (e.g., "Exact via JDT full resolution" vs. "Exact via clangd without compile_commands.json"), preserving tier provenance the way CHA/RTA/points-to results always carry their algorithm name — never collapse `Exact` into one undifferentiated bucket."

Both are refinements to the enum's granularity, not evidence that the three-lifetime shape itself is wrong — I looked specifically for a backend that fits none of the three and didn't find one."

69	        "critique": "## Verdict: Real hazard, but it refines the design rather than breaking it

**The hazard is real and the trait sketch as described doesn't address it.** `WorkspaceIndex::build`'s `par_iter` means N worker threads could call into one warm `Session` resource concurrently. A `PrecisionUpgrader` implementation that stores the resource as, say, `Arc<Mutex<ChildProcess>>` and does "write request to stdin, blocking-read matching response from stdout" inside the lock would be actively wrong, not just slow: multiple threads racing on one stdio pipe can cross-wire which response belongs to which request unless something demultiplexes by request ID, and a coarse mutex around the whole round-trip serializes everything the parallel analysis was trying to buy.

**Real precedent doesn't point to "single-threaded actor" as a blanket answer — it points to a snapshot/MVCC discipline, with client-side multiplexing bolted on top for the LSP-speaking backends.** rust-analyzer's own `GlobalState` is the clearest evidence: it does not serialize reads through one queue. Each request clones `Arc`s into an immutable `GlobalStateSnapshot`, so concurrent reads proceed against a frozen world while a single writer thread advances the real state; Salsa's revision counter (with the volatile/durable durability split) means an in-flight query gets cancelled (`Cancelled::throw`) rather than racing if a write lands underneath it. gopls's Session→View→Snapshot hierarchy is architecturally the same idea from a different codebase: Snapshot is immutable per-edit, and reads fan out against a frozen Snapshot rather than a live mutable index. Neither system is "single-threaded actor" in the request-queue sense — both allow real read concurrency — but both achieve it specifically by *not* exposing raw mutable shared state, which a naive `PrecisionUpgrader::promote(&self, ...)` over a bare handle would.

**Where an actor/queue pattern legitimately does appear** is at the transport layer for the LSP-speaking backends monokl would drive as subprocesses (gopls, jdtls, kotlin-lsp, Metals, clangd). JSON-RPC over one stdio pipe needs exactly one owner reading stdout and demuxing by request ID back to whichever caller is waiting — this is precisely what `async-lsp`/`tower-lsp`-style clients implement: a single connection-owning task, worker threads submit requests through a channel and await a response via a oneshot keyed on request ID. The fix isn't a redesign, it's a contract: all Salsa inputs must be loaded in a single-threaded "prime" phase before the resource is handed to parallel readers; the `PrecisionUpgrader::promote` call itself must be read-only against the resource. Kotlin's evidence (JetBrains' own backlog tracking memory-accumulation "under long-running parallel analysis" of Analysis API sessions) is corroborating, independent evidence that hammering a warm semantic resource with full worker-pool parallelism is a real reliability risk even when it's "just" reads.

**No radical, incompatible restructuring found.** I specifically checked for one — a case where Session's real concurrency model couldn't be expressed as "a thread-safe handle, primed once, read concurrently" — and didn't find it. The fix is additive: require `Session` resources be `Send + Sync` handles, mandate a write/prime phase separate from the parallel read phase, and, for LSP backends, mandate the connection-actor pattern internally. That's a refinement to the resource's implied contract, not a fork of `PrecisionUpgrader`/`LanguageAnalyzer`."

72	    "synthesis": "# monokl Daemon-Tier Architecture: Final Recommendation

## 1. Verdict: Amended, not confirmed as-is

The **lifetime enum survives unchanged** — every backend researched (TS/tsserver-tsgo, Rust/rust-analyzer, Python/Pyrefly-ty, Go/gopls, Java/jdtls, Kotlin/kotlin-lsp, Scala/Metals, C++/clangd, C#/Roslyn, Ruby/Sorbet-Solargraph) maps cleanly onto PerCall, PerInvocation, or Session as a *ceiling* on affordable call frequency. No language demanded a fourth duration tier. That part of the draft is confirmed.

Three concrete amendments are required before this ships as spec, each tied to a specific, independently-corroborated finding:

**(a) `PrecisionUpgrader::upgrade()` must not return a bare `CapabilityPrecision`.** The data-model-fit critique found this independently across Kotlin (`KaErrorCallInfo{candidates, diagnostic}`), Go (confirmed-vs-candidate satisfaction), Scala (two orthogonal axes: resolved-value precision vs. provenance precision), Rust (trait predicates/dyn-compatibility), and C++ (RecoveryExpr's preserved partial structure) — five independent language studies converging on the same gap is the strongest signal in this whole research round. The return type must be an outcome carrying: a possibly-unresolved precision tier, a per-language-typed extension payload, and room for multiple ranked/ambiguous candidates rather than one collapsed answer. This is a correctness fix, not a nice-to-have — collapsing Kotlin's candidate set or Go's confirmed/candidate split into one enum value manufactures false confidence the upstream tool never claimed, directly violating the stated priority against hallucination-inducing omissions.

**(b) Lifetime is a property of each resource an upgrader holds, not one field per trait impl.** The process-lifecycle-fit critique is exact: rust-analyzer's own `proc-macro-srv-cli` is a supervised subprocess living *inside* an otherwise-PerInvocation Salsa build. A flat `lifetime: PerInvocation` can't express "this upgrader also owns a nested Session-like sub-resource." Fix: an upgrader declares a set of typed sub-resources, each with its own lifetime, rather than being forced into one lifetime bucket (or, as C++ shows, split into two separate trait impls — acceptable but not the only correct shape).

**(c) `Session` must distinguish owned vs. attached.** gopls's real production model (`-remote=auto`) and kotlin-lsp's RocksDB persistence both attach to a resource monokl doesn't spawn or fully control — different failure surface (stale daemon, version mismatch, no daemon present) than "monokl's host constructs and holds a handle." This is an orthogonal ownership axis on top of the duration axis, not a new duration.

The performance-concurrency-fit critique does **not** require a design change beyond a documented contract: `Session` resources must be `Send + Sync` handles with a single-threaded prime/load phase before parallel read access, and LSP-speaking backends must be wrapped in a connection-actor (one task owns stdio, demuxes by request ID) — this is implementation discipline, not a trait fork.

## 2. Per-language table

| Language | Real backend | Lifetime fit | What must not be flattened |
|---|---|---|---|
| TypeScript/JS | tsserver / tsgo (TS 7.0 LSP) | PerCall unusable (whole-program load dominates cost); **PerInvocation** viable stopgap; **Session** is the tool's native mode | The genuine-`any` vs. gave-up-and-defaulted-to-`any` distinction — invisible unless the separate opt-in suggestion-diagnostics channel is deliberately correlated by span |
| Rust | ra_ap_hir / Salsa | **PerInvocation** (fresh Salsa DB, memoizes across one run) as default; **Session** matches real LSP GlobalState; nested PerCall/Session proc-macro sub-resource inside either | Trait predicates, dyn-compatibility violations, generic monomorphization (`GenericSubstitution`) — real solver output, not string matching |
| Python | Pyrefly / ty | Both are subprocess/LSP citizens despite being Rust-native — no embeddable API exists; **PerInvocation** works, but **Session** is where their Salsa/incremental advantage actually pays off | The categorical `Any`/`Unknown` distinction (not a confidence score) — map directly, don't invent a scalar |
| Go | gopls | PerCall untenable (cold start 10s–3m+ documented); PerInvocation only marginal; **Session, attached** (thin forwarder to gopls's own `-remote` daemon, not monokl-owned) | Confirmed (local, real `go/types` assignability) vs. candidate (global method-set-fingerprint) interface satisfaction — gopls itself never unifies these |
| Java | jdtls / JDT Core | PerCall non-viable; PerInvocation **fragile** (batched Maven import OOM-crashes past ~3000 files — not a graceful degrade); **Session** only lifetime that amortizes cost, needs an explicit project-size gate | `IBinding.isRecovered()` — a real, queryable "this is a fabricated placeholder" flag that exists on JDT's Core API but is not exposed through jdtls's LSP surface |
| Kotlin | kotlin-lsp (full IntelliJ) or standalone Analysis API | PerCall rules itself out (GB-scale, seconds-to-minutes even for a single init); **Session with recycling/health contract** (bounded by staleness/memory budget — unbounded warm sessions leak per JetBrains' own tracker) | `KaErrorCallInfo{candidateCalls, diagnostic}` ambiguity, `SMARTCAST_IMPOSSIBLE` diagnostics, flexible/platform types (`T!`) — all first-class sealed/typed signals, must map to an `Ambiguous{candidates}` shape, not a binary |
| Scala | Metals (mtags + BSP + presentation compiler) | PerCall/PerInvocation both repay a 10s–15min build import; **Session-only in practice** | Implicit argument/conversion resolution — two independently-scored axes (resolved value vs. provenance), since Metals can be confidently wrong about *why* |
| C/C++ | Clang subprocess (PerCall) *and* clangd (Session) as **two separate impls** | **PerCall**: clang-ast, genuinely cheap per-TU; **Session**: clangd background index, hours-scale cold start, only viable warm | RecoveryExpr's preserved partial subexpressions/dependent types — carry as extension payload, not a precision bump |
| C# | Roslyn (OmniSharp / csharp-ls / MS server) | **PerInvocation**/**Session**, standard workspace-load-then-reuse; no architectural surprise | (Not deeply differentiated in research — verify redistribution licensing on MS's official server before depending on it) |
| Ruby | Sorbet (near-zero fixed cold start via compiled-in stdlib blob) vs. Solargraph | **PerCall is genuinely viable for Sorbet** — the one real exception to "PerCall is a trap" | Fixed cold-start cost is uniquely cheap; project-size-proportional check time still applies, don't oversell it |
| PHP | Intelephense | PerInvocation/Session, standard shape | Licensing (proprietary premium tier), not architecture, is the real constraint |

## 3. Ingestion-model recommendation

Extend the existing shared-envelope/per-language-variant pattern (`FileAnalysis` → `LangData::{TypeScript, Rust, Java, ...}`) — do not merge daemon output into it. Following the SCIP/CodeQL/LSP-capability precedent directly: add `daemon_extension: Option<DaemonExtension>` as a sibling field alongside the existing base `LangData` payload, where `DaemonExtension` is itself a per-language enum (`Rust(RustTraitFacts)`, `Java(ClasspathFacts)`, `Kotlin(SmartCastFacts)`, `Go(SatisfactionFacts{confirmed, candidate})`, `Scala(ImplicitFacts{value_precision, provenance_precision})`, `Cpp(RecoveryFacts)`, …). Each per-language extension variant carries whatever richly-typed structure that language's finding demands (candidate lists, dual precision axes, recovered-binding flags) — never coerced through a shared generic field set.

`CapabilityPrecision` stays as the base analyzer's own honest self-report (Unsupported/Heuristic/Structural/Exact) and is **left untouched by the presence of a daemon_extension** — the extension is additive provenance, not a replacement value. When an extension is present, it carries its own `PrecisionUpgradeOutcome` (tier reached + backend/operation identity + per-language typed payload), mirroring the CHA/RTA/points-to discipline of tagging the producing algorithm and never letting it be silently erased. This makes absence (no upgrader ran, Session unavailable, project gated by size) safe and silent by construction — exactly the LSP "ignore capabilities you don't understand" property — and keeps `TraitImplIndex`-style per-language indexes as the natural home for the language-specific facts inside each extension variant, rather than inventing a new generic index type.

## 4. Confidence-signaling rules

Before any `PrecisionUpgrader` promotes a result toward `Exact`, it must:

1. **Never trust protocol silence.** A missing `ResponseError` or absent diagnostic proves nothing — LSP has no wire-level field for "resolved to a degraded fallback" (verified directly against the 3.17 spec's `Location`/`Hover`/`ResponseError` shapes).
2. **Prefer native/extended APIs that expose the backend's own confidence bit** over plain LSP: JDT `IBinding.isRecovered()`, Kotlin's `KaErrorCallInfo` sealed type, clangd's `textDocument/ast` extension (RecoveryExpr/`contains-errors`), TS's separate opt-in suggestion-diagnostics channel. Plain LSP structurally cannot carry these signals even when the compiler computed them internally.
3. **Maintain a per-backend sentinel denylist** checked on every promotion: JDT `isRecovered()==true`; Clang dependent/recovery type strings or diagnostics at/upstream of the span; TS hover text of bare `any` not matching an explicit source annotation; Kotlin `T!` platform-type markers or `SMARTCAST_IMPOSSIBLE`; Scala ambiguous-implicit notices; Go's global-algorithm-only matches (cap those at `candidate`, never `confirmed`).
4. **When only generic LSP is available and no sentinel exists**, cap at `Structural` if the file has any diagnostic at or upstream of the queried location, and emit an explicit monokl diagnostic explaining the downgrade rather than guessing.
5. **Tag every Exact/upgraded result with backend + operation identity** (e.g., "Exact via JDT full resolution" vs. "Exact via clangd, no compile_commands.json") — never an undifferentiated Exact bucket, per the CHA/RTA/points-to precedent of preserving which algorithm produced a fact.

## 5. Genuinely uncertain, not papered over

- No rigorous data exists on what fraction of Java symbol references are external-JAR-only (the Snyk bytecode-LOC figure is a different metric and shouldn't be repurposed).
- Microsoft's official C# language server's redistribution/licensing terms outside VS Code were not confirmed this round.
- Rust's public API exposes no explicit "multiple equally-valid candidates" variant for trait-method ambiguity distinct from Kotlin's — this may be a real gap in `ra_ap_hir` itself, not just unresearched.
- TS 7.0's embeddable programmatic API (promised for 7.1) doesn't exist yet; today's integration must go through LSP JSON-RPC only — revisit this recommendation when 7.1 ships.
- Sourcegraph's own historical live-langserver-then-pivot-to-SCIP narrative was not independently re-verified this round (relied on general knowledge, not a freshly checked source).
- Whether Session's owned-vs-attached split needs its own enum variant or can stay a boolean/metadata flag on `Session` was not stress-tested against an actual implementation — treat as an open detail, not a resolved one."
